sets.title: Changes in energy
sets.sourceHeading: Question (SD; Calculate; Combined science)	Changes in energy
sets.questionHtml:
01 The ZARM Drop Tower at the University of Bremen in Germany is a 120 m tall vacuum tube, where experiments into the effects of microgravity conditions experienced in orbit can be carried out. Figure 1 shows how the tower works.

Figure 1

Experiments can be carried out inside the drop capsule when it is dropped from the top of the tower, or it can be fired upwards by the catapult at the bottom. The drop capsule safely falls into the deceleration unit at the bottom of the tower, which is full of tiny polystyrene beads that safely absorb all the drop capsule’s kinetic energy on impact.

01.1 Write down the equation that links the kinetic energy, mass and speed of an object.

[1 mark]

01.2 Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the drop capsule immediately after firing in
catapult mode.

[3 marks]

Maximum kinetic energy of drop capsule in catapult mode = J

01.3 Explain why the energy transferred to the surroundings is zero while the drop capsule is travelling up and down the tower.

[2 marks]

01.4 As no energy is transferred to the surroundings, use your answer to 01.2 to calculate the maximum height that the drop capsule can travel in catapult mode. Use this value to explain why the height of the tower is 120 m.

Use the equation:

gravitational potential energy = mass × gravitational field strength × height

Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg

[5 marks]

sets.title: Specific heat capacity
sets.sourceHeading: Question (LD; Plan; Combined science)	Specific heat capacity
sets.questionHtml:
02 Water is used in radiator heating systems because it is a liquid and it can be easily pumped around. It also has a very high specific heat capacity, so it will cool down slowly as it is
pumped around.

Plan an experiment to determine the specific heat capacity of water.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
02 Water is used in radiator heating systems because it is a liquid and it can be easily pumped around. It also has a very high specific heat capacity, so it will cool down slowly as it is
pumped around.

Plan an experiment to determine the specific heat capacity of water.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref.

02

Level 3: The method would lead to the production of a valid outcome. The key steps are identified and logically sequenced.

5–6

AO1

4.1.1.3

Level 2: The method would not necessarily lead to a valid outcome. Most steps are identified, but the method is not fully logically sequenced.

3–4

Level 1: The method would not lead to a valid outcome. Some relevant steps are identified, but links are not made clear.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Specific heat capacity is related to change in thermal energy, mass and temperature change through the equation:

Change in thermal energy =
mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change

∆E=mc∆θ

This can be re-arranged to give:

c=∆Em×∆θ

A 250 cm3 glass beaker is wrapped in insulating material such as bubble wrap and held in place with a rubber band.

The mass of the beaker and insulation is measured and recorded using a balance.

200 cm3 of water is added to the beaker, and the new mass is measured and recorded. The mass of the water is then calculated.

A 12 V electrical heater is placed in the water through a suitable lid such as Petri dish with a hole cut in it.

The 12 V heater is connected to a joulemeter, which is in turn connected to a 12 V power supply.

A thermometer is put into the beaker through a second hole in the lid, and the temperature of the water is measured and recorded.

The power supply is turned on and the experiment is left on for 10 minutes, stirring regularly before being switched off.

After 10 minutes, the electrical energy measured on the joulemeter is recorded and the final temperature is measured and recorded.

The values are substituted into the rearranged equation above and the specific heat capacity calculated in J/kg °C

The apparatus is allowed to cool, then the procedure is repeated twice more and a mean value is calculated.
sets.modelHtml:
02 1. Wrap a beaker in bubble wrap and place a lid on. This is for insulation.

2. Measure the total mass.

3. Remove the lid and pour water in the beaker so it is about two-thirds full. Put the lid back on and find the new mass.

4. Use the results to find the mass of the water. This is m.

5. Measure the temperature of the water. Connect an electrical heater to a joulemeter.

6. Put the heater into the water with the thermometer. Make holes in the lid to put
them through.

7. Switch on the heater and wait for the temperature to rise by 20°C. Stir
the water while you are heating it.

8. Turn off the heater and record the reading on the joulemeter. This is ∆E.

9. Rearrange ∆E=mc∆θ

To give c= ∆E/m∆θ. Use ∆θ=20.
sets.partialHtml:
02 1. Measure the mass of the water and then pour into a beaker.

2. Connect up the electrical heater to a joulemeter and then to a power supply.

3. Put the heater into the beaker with a thermometer. Measure the temperature of
the water.

4. Turn on the heater and leave it to heat up the water for 10 minutes. Keep stirring
the water.

5. After 10 minutes, turn off the heater and measure the reading on the joulemeter and the temperature of the water.

6. Calculate the specific heat capacity of the water using the equation:

Change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change

∆E=mc∆θ

This answer clearly meets many of the criteria for a Level 2 answer. The method would lead to a valid answer, as most of the steps are included that will calculate an answer, but some key elements are missing, such as the insulation around the beaker and using a lid. The equation needed is stated but not rearranged to show how to calculate c. The answer does not include how to measure the mass of the water, so it is insufficiently detailed.

3 out of 6 marks awarded.

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref.

03

Level 2: Scientifically relevant features are identified; the way(s) in which they are similar/different is made clear and (where appropriate) the magnitude of the similarity/difference is noted.

4–6

AO3

4.1.2.1

WS 3.3

WS 3.5

Level 1: Relevant features are identified and differences noted.

1–3

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

The insulation material needs to be damp proof as the house is beside the sea.

This excludes cellulose and hemp.

Calculating payback times for the other materials:

wood wool ⟹200×£19£30= 127 years

cork ⟹200×£20£70= 57 years

sheep’s wool ⟹200×£20£85= 47 years

From payback times, sheep’s wool and cork would seem to be the best choices.

Sheep’s wool is the best insulator, because it has the lowest thermal conductivity, but cork is quite close to it. Wood wool is a much worse insulator because its thermal conductivity is very high.

Considering some of the other properties of cork and sheep’s wool; cork has better sound proofing than sheep’s wool.

Cork has a very low carbon footprint, whereas sheep’s wool only has a low carbon footprint.

Cork would be the best choice, because it has a low payback time, is damp proof, has high sound proofing and a very low carbon footprint.

OR

Sheep’s wool would be the best choice because it has the shortest payback time.
sets.modelHtml:
03 In order to decide which one is best I need to calculate the payback times for each one:

cellulose ⟹200×£15£74= 41 years

wood wool ⟹200×£19£30= 127 years

cork ⟹200×£20£70= 57 years

hemp ⟹200×£16£76= 42 years

sheep’s wool ⟹200×£20£85= 47 years

This suggests that cellulose would be the best because it has the shortest payback time. However, the building is next to the sea so it will be damp and wet a lot. This means that cellulose and hemp are not suitable as they are not suitable for damp rooms. This leaves wood wool, cork and sheep’s wool. The payback time for wood wool is very long and it has the highest thermal conductivity, so it is the worst insulator.

Cork has a very low carbon footprint compared to that of sheep’s wool and it is a better sound insulator, which might be important next to the sea.

I would choose cork, even though it has a slightly longer payback time than sheep’s wool. Its other properties are better than sheep’s wool.
sets.partialHtml:
03 Cellulose and hemp would not be suitable as the house is too damp. The payback times for the other materials are:

wood wool ⟹200 × £19£30= 127 years

cork ⟹200 × £20£70= 57 years

sheep’s wool ⟹200 ×£20£85 = 47 years

The sheep’s wool has the shortest payback time so that is the one to go for.

The student’s answer takes account of the need for the material to be suitable for a damp location and has correctly eliminated two of the options on this basis. They have then correctly calculated the feedback times for the other materials. Two features have been referred to and the magnitude of difference identified, so the answer is in Level 2. However, other factors influencing the choice have not been referred to, so although the choice is justified it doesn’t use all the available evidence.

4 out of 6 marks awarded.

Level 1: Relevant features are identified and differences noted.

1–3

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Answer must include comparison of both groups and point out exceptions.

Similarities

Both groups involve ugly land use.

Differences

Fossil fuels produce air pollution, which can lead to global warming or acid rain.

Total air pollution from fossil fuels = 2250 kg/MWh

Zero net air pollution from renewable sources

All fossil fuel sources use large volumes of water. Only hydroelectric/biomass renewables use large volumes of water. Water extraction reduces the amount of water available for wildlife habitats and for human consumption.

All fossil fuels sources affect aquatic life. Only hydroelectric and biomass affect aquatic life.

All fossil fuels sources produce polluting and warming water discharges. Only biomass produces polluting and warming water discharges. Most renewables do not produce any water discharges. Water pollution can lead to the destruction of habitats, as can warm water.

Most fossil fuels produce solid waste (not gas). Only biomass produces solid waste. Solid wastes are mostly sent to landfill and can then pollute the environment.

Fossil fuel extraction impacts on the environmental use of land. Only hydroelectric affects land use significantly.
sets.modelHtml:
04 Polluting gases: Burning fossil fuels releases NOx and SO2, which cause acid rain, and CO2, which increases global warming (2250 kg/MWh overall), but renewables don’t produce any air pollution or greenhouse gases.

Some solid pollutants are produced when oil and coal are burned but not with gas. Some of these are toxic and so harm or may kill wildlife. Of the renewables, only biomass produces solid waste, but this is not toxic.

Using fossil fuel resources needs large volumes of water, whereas only hydroelectric and biomass use large volumes of water.

The discharge water from power stations that burn fossil fuels contains pollutants. Of the renewables, only biomass produces water pollution. Fossil fuel power stations also release warm water into the environment, which can affect aquatic life. Of the renewables, only biomass releases warm water, although hydroelectric power plants can harm aquatic life and also cause habitat damage when valleys are flooded.

Renewables and fossil fuels can all cause visual pollution. Wind turbines are usually built in the countryside and look ugly. The scale of solar panels and wind turbines needed for power supply means they take up a lot of land, whereas the fossil fuel power stations look ugly but take up less land.

Only the fossil fuels need mining, which can destroy habitats for wildlife.
sets.partialHtml:
04 The fossil fuels are coal, oil and gas. The renewables are hydroelectric, biomass, solar and wind.

The main similarity between them is that all of the energy sources create ugly buildings, which are not nice to look at.

Fossil fuels produce large amounts of air pollution. Air pollution from carbon dioxide leads to global warming. Only burning biomass produces air pollution.

Fossil fuels use lots of water resources and affect aquatic life. Taking lots of water from rivers can cause the destruction of animal habitats. Hydroelectric and biomass also use a lot of water resources but solar and wind do not.

Fossil fuels can pollute the environment, some of the pollution is toxic and it can heat the environment, also destroying habitats.

Most of the fossil fuels produce solid waste, whereas only biomass does from the renewables. The solid waste is probably put into landfill.

The student has picked out most of the key features and has given some form of scientific background to them. This is Level 2. Not all of the indicative content has been considered, but there are similarities and differences, which is also Level 2. Unfortunately, the answer does not include the use of the figures for air pollution, so this does not score full marks.

4 out of 6 marks awarded.

05 A new campsite is looking to install a renewable energy system in order to power the site. Wind power and solar power are being considered.

Key data

The campsite is already connected to the National Grid.

The campsite is open from April to October and is closed for maintenance during the winter.

During the summer months, the peak electrical energy consumption by the site is about
400 kW, and during the winter it is about 5 kW.

The site has a large open field next to the campsite with an area of 5000 m2.

The solar panels suggested can produce 250 W and have an area of 1.5 m2.

The 11 kW wind turbines suggested have a height of 18 m and require 200 m2 per turbine.

Evaluate this data and suggest which energy source would be best for the campsite to use.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
05 A new campsite is looking to install a renewable energy system in order to power the site. Wind power and solar power are being considered.

Key data

The campsite is already connected to the National Grid.

The campsite is open from April to October and is closed for maintenance during the winter.

During the summer months, the peak electrical energy consumption by the site is about
400 kW, and during the winter it is about 5 kW.

The site has a large open field next to the campsite with an area of 5000 m2.

The solar panels suggested can produce 250 W and have an area of 1.5 m2.

The 11 kW wind turbines suggested have a height of 18 m and require 200 m2 per turbine.

Evaluate this data and suggest which energy source would be best for the campsite to use.

[6 marks]

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref.

Level 3: A judgement, strongly linked and logically supported by a sufficient range of correct reasons, is given.

5–6

WS 1.3, 1.4

Indicative content

A judgement (giving a suggested energy source) should be made, with evidence for AND against considered.

The peak energy demand of the campsite will occur during the summer months, either first thing in the morning, or more likely during the evening when people are cooking, eating and needing lighting.

Solar power only provides energy when it is daylight. Solar power will not provide any energy during darkness and twilight.

Wind power only provides energy when the wind is blowing. During the summer months the reliability of the wind to provide enough energy is poor.

As such neither of these energy sources will provide 100% of the campsite energy.

In terms of peak demand:

Maximum power output of solar panels

=area of fieldarea of panel×power of panel

=50001.5×250=833 333 W=833 kW

This is greater than the peak energy consumption of the campsite (400 kW), so some energy can be sold back to the National Grid.

Maximum power output of wind turbines:

=area of fieldarea of turbine×power of turbine

=5000200×11=275 kW

This is not enough to power the campsite at peak consumption.

The only power source that can provide coverage of peak power consumption is the solar panels.

Both systems will use up the area of the field. Campers may not prefer to camp next to 25 wind turbines as they are more unsightly and would make more noise.

Energy from the National Grid would be needed at times for the campsite with both energy sources.

The suggested power source to use is solar panels.
sets.modelHtml:
05 If the whole field were covered with solar panels, total power generated would be:

250 W × 5000 m2/1.5 m2 = 833 333 W

If the whole field were used for wind turbines, total power generated would be:

11 kW × 5000 m2/200 m2 = 275 kW

Solar panels have a greater possible power output, which is enough to meet the campsite’s peak needs in summer (400 kW), whereas wind power would not be enough for peak demand in summer.

However, solar panels only produce electricity when the sun is shining, so no power generated at night. Also, the power generated in spring and autumn when hours of daylight are less will be much less than 250 W per panel. So some power will be needed from the National Grid – more in winter than summer and always at night.

Wind turbines only produce power when it is windy but the weather is variable so the peak output of 275 kW won’t always be achieved and could be zero. Although there could be power generated at night, some power will always be needed from the National Grid, especially in summer when it is less windy and when demand is highest.

Campers may not like having to look at the tall wind turbines in the field next door and they may be noisy.

I think the campsite should choose solar panels.
sets.partialHtml:

=50001.5×250=833 333 W=833 kW

Maximum power output of wind turbines:

=5000200×11=275 kW

As the campsite needs 400 kW at its peak consumption, the only energy source that can do this is the solar panels.

The problem with solar panels is that they don’t make power when it’s dark, and wind turbines don’t make power when the wind is not blowing.

The campsite will have to run on electricity from the National Grid when it is dark or if it’s not windy. During the winter, the spare energy generated can be sold to the National Grid to cover this.

I think the campsite should choose solar panels for its energy supply.

This is Level 3. There are sufficient reasons to make the judgement given but the level of detail given is not sufficient for a top Level 3 mark.

sets.questionHtml:
06 Table 5 lists some of the issues associated with the production of electricity from nuclear power and renewable energy generation.

Table 5

Renewable energy

Nuclear power

Renewables contribute about 33% of UK electricity. To meet climate change targets the UK is committed to increasing the proportion of energy generated by renewables.

Nuclear power contributes approximately 20% of UK electricity. It is projected that this will fall to about 10% before 2030.

Renewables generate electricity from energy transferred from the Sun.

Nuclear power generates electricity from the nuclear energy stored within nuclear fuel using the process of nuclear fission.

Renewable energy does not produce hazardous waste products.

Nuclear fission produces waste products, some of which will remain radioactive for millions of years.

Renewable energy produces no net carbon dioxide during the generation of electricity, although carbon dioxide is produced by some biofuel processes, and considerable amounts are produced during the production of large-scale projects such as the construction of dams or tidal barrages.

Nuclear power does not produce a significant amount of carbon dioxide during its lifetime generating electricity.

Significant amounts of carbon dioxide are produced during the construction and decommissioning phases of a nuclear power plant.

Renewable energy is variable; for example, solar energy is not generated at night and wind energy is not produced when there is no wind.

Nuclear power provides considerable security of our energy supply as it is always on, and is likely to remain as a part of the energy mix into the medium-term future.

Compare the issues associated with the production of electricity from nuclear power and renewable energy.

[6 marks]

Level 2: Scientifically relevant features are identified, the way(s) in which they are similar/different is made clear and (where appropriate) the magnitude of the similarity/difference is noted.

No relevant content

Indicative content

Answer must include comparison of the similarities and differences between the generation of electricity by nuclear power and renewable energy.

Similarities

Renewable energy and nuclear power do not produce significant amounts of CO2 during the production of electricity.

Some forms of renewable energy and nuclear power produce significant amounts of CO2 during the construction and decommissioning of facilities.

Differences

Renewable energies produce 33% of UK electricity compared to 20% by nuclear power. This is 13% more.

In the future the difference will get bigger as less electricity is generated via nuclear power and more is generated via renewable energy.

As renewable energy is generated from the Sun, it will continue to be produced. Nuclear power is produced by the nuclear fission of nuclear fuels such as uranium ore. This is a finite resource and will eventually run out.

The radioactive waste products from nuclear power will remain dangerous for millions of years and will need very secure storage. Renewable energy does not produce any hazardous waste.

Nuclear power is a very secure (predictable) power supply that will be needed into the medium term because many forms of renewable energy are variable in their power output, so a more reliable source is needed to ensure continuous supply.
sets.modelHtml:
06 Producing electricity from renewables or from nuclear fuel is similar in terms of contribution to climate change, as in both cases no net carbon dioxide is produced.

There is a difference in environmental impact: renewables do not result in hazardous waste, but radioactive waste is produced from the generation of electricity by nuclear fuels. This waste is a long-term problem due to the long half-lives of the waste.

Another difference is reliability and availability. Nuclear power stations produce a constant power output and can be sited in any area where there is a good water supply, but some renewables – such as wind turbines and solar panels – don’t generate power in all weather conditions or reliably in all areas.

The source of energy for most renewables is ultimately the Sun (except for tidal power) but the source for nuclear energy is radioactive rocks. However, nuclear fuels are a very concentrated form of energy, so despite nuclear fuels being non-renewable they are not likely to run out soon.

There is a difference in percentage of our energy produced from renewables – more (33%) is currently from renewables than nuclear (20%) and the difference will increase in future because the percentage from renewables will increase and the percentage from nuclear will decrease.
sets.partialHtml:
06 Renewable energy and nuclear power are similar because neither of them produce much carbon dioxide gas when they are making electricity.

They are different because they contribute different amounts of the UK electricity supply. Renewable energy contributes more than nuclear power.

They are also different because they generate electricity in different ways. Renewable energy generates electricity from the Sun, which will carry on forever, but nuclear power uses nuclear fuel, which will eventually run out.

Nuclear power produces hazardous waste, whereas renewable energy does not.

Nuclear power is secure as it can be produced all the time. Some forms of renewable energy do not generate electricity all the time.

The student has made several, scientifically relevant comparative comments. The answer is at least Level 2. However, the student has not compared the numerical values given about the proportion of UK electricity generated from each source, so this is not a top Level 3 answer.

5 out of 6 marks awarded.

Plan an experiment, involving a voltmeter and an ammeter, to investigate how the resistance of a nichrome wire depends upon its length.

Circuit diagram:

Correct symbols needed for ammeter, voltmeter, power supply or battery/cell) needed.

Diagram/text should also show crocodile clips, metre ruler and nichrome wire.

Method

Attach the wire connector with a crocodile clip to the nichrome wire at 0 m on the ruler.

Attach the second connecting wire with a crocodile clip to the nichrome wire at 20 cm on the ruler.

Measure and record the current and potential difference.

Calculate the resistance: resistance=potential differencecurrent

Repeat steps 2 and 3 for 40 cm, 60 cm, 80 cm and 100 cm lengths of nichrome.

Reducing uncertainties

Repeat the experiment twice more and calculate mean values.
sets.modelHtml:
07 Set up the circuit like this.

Use crocodile clips at the end of leads to attach them to the nichrome wire.

Place a metre ruler along the wire so that the zero mark is at the first crocodile clip. Move the second crocodile clip so that there is 20 cm of wire between the clips.

Switch on the power pack and measure the p.d. across the wire (in volts) and the current in the circuit (in amps).

Calculate resistance using resistance=potential differencecurrent.

Turn off the power pack and increase the length of wire between the crocodile clips to
40 cm. Repeat the measurements.

Repeat steps 3 to 5 until there are sets of measurements at 20 cm, 40 cm, 60 cm, 80 cm and 100 cm.

To reduce uncertainty, repeat the measurements for each length of wire twice. Find the mean resistance at each length.
sets.partialHtml:

Set the crocodile clips 10 cm apart.

Measure the current and the voltage.

Calculate the resistance.

Move one crocodile clip so that its now 20 cm apart and repeat the measurements.

Do it again every 10 cm up to 1 m.

Repeat the experiment and calculate an average.

This method would not necessarily lead to a valid outcome because the student has used the term ‘average’ rather than ‘mean’, so the calculated value may not be correct. sets.questionHtml:
09 Heating resistors are large resistors made from ceramic materials. They are designed to be used as heating elements in devices such as hair tongs. One particular pair of hair tongs has three different combinations of resistors, arranged as shown in Figure 3. Each combination produces a different heat setting.

Each resistor has a resistance of 4 ohms.

Figure 3

The heating effect depends upon the total resistance of the combination of resistors.

The three heat settings are hot, medium and cool.

Calculate the total resistance of combination 1 and then state if the total resistance of combinations 2 and 3 have a higher or lower resistance than combination 1.

Suggest which combination should be used for each heat setting.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
09 Heating resistors are large resistors made from ceramic materials. They are designed to be used as heating elements in devices such as hair tongs. One particular pair of hair tongs has three different combinations of resistors, arranged as shown in Figure 3. Each combination produces a different heat setting.

Each resistor has a resistance of 4 ohms.

Figure 3

The heating effect depends upon the total resistance of the combination of resistors.

The three heat settings are hot, medium and cool.

Calculate the total resistance of combination 1 and then state if the total resistance of combinations 2 and 3 have a higher or lower resistance than combination 1.

Suggest which combination should be used for each heat setting.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref.

09

Combination 1 – all in series

RT=R1+R2+R3

RT=4+4+4

= 12 Ω

Combination 2 – all in parallel

Total resistance will be less than the smallest resistance, which is 4 Ω.

Combination 3 – two in parallel with the third in series

The total resistance of the two in parallel will be less than 4 Ω, so

the total resistance of 4 Ω in series with the two in parallel will be greater than 4 but less than 8.

Heat loss from a resistor is proportional to the resistance
(P=I2R)

So:

Hot = combination 1

Medium = combination 3

Cool = combination 2

1

1

1

1

1

1

AO2

4.2.2

WS 3.3
sets.modelHtml:
09 Total resistance of combination 1 = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 ohms

In combination 2 all 3 resistors are in parallel, so total resistance is less than any of the resistors by itself. <4 ohms

In combination 3 one of the resistors in series with a combination of 2 resistors in parallel. Combination of the two 4 ohm resistances in parallel is less than 4 ohms.

Total resistance in combination 3 is 4 ohms plus a value <4 ohms: between 4 and 8 ohms.

Heating effect depends on power loss in resistor. P = I2R

Therefore, cool setting (least power loss) for lowest resistance, combination 2, hot setting combination 1 and medium combination 3.
sets.partialHtml:
09 Total resistance of Combination 1 = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 ohms.

I think that Combination 2 will have the lowest resistance because the resistors are all in parallel, so the combined resistance will be lower than the lowest value of resistor in the combination, which is 4 Ω.

Combination 3 will be greater than 2 but less than 1. The highest setting on the tongs should be the combination with the highest resistance because P=I2R, so the bigger R is, the bigger the power, so the hotter it will be. The low setting will be the one with the lowest setting and the medium setting will be the one in the middle.

high setting = combination 1

medium setting = combination 3

low setting = combination 2

1 mark is awarded for calculating the total resistance of Combination 1. 1 mark is awarded for the statement about the total resistance of Combination 2 will be less than the lowest resistance in the combination. Although suggesting that Combination 3 will be in the middle is correct, there is no reasoning, so no marks are awarded for this. 1 mark is given for the correct reasoning about power being related to R and 1 mark is awarded for the suggested
heat settings.

5 out of 6 marks awarded.

sets.questionHtml:
11 Many businesses have back-up power systems so that if there is a power cut, critical systems such as lighting, remain on. Figure 20 shows one such system.

Figure 20

Under normal circumstances, the lights are powered from the mains supply, and the battery unit is kept fully charged. If a power cut occurs, the mains supply is cut off and the battery unit takes over, powering the lights for a short period of time.

Explain the energy transfers involved with this system:

under normal circumstances

during a power cut.

You can ignore the differences between stores of energy involved with various ways of producing mains electricity.

[6 marks]

parts.html:

under normal circumstances

during a power cut.

You can ignore the differences between stores of energy involved with various ways of producing mains electricity.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref.

11

Level 3: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, given in detail and logically linked to form a clear account.

5–6

AO2

4.4.1.1

4.2.4.2

Level 2: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, and there are attempts at logically linking. The resulting account is not fully clear.

3–4

Level 1: Points are identified and stated simply, but their relevance is not clear and there is no attempt at logical linking.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Under normal circumstances:

Energy is transferred from the power station to the environment by electricity, light and heat.

Energy is transferred from the mains by electrical work as electrical charge moves due to a potential difference.

The flow of charge is an electrical current; this carries energy.

Some of the energy transferred by electricity from the mains is stored in the battery unit.

During a power cut:

Energy stored in the battery unit is transferred as electrical work to the internal energy of the surroundings by heating and radiation.
sets.modelHtml:
11 Under normal circumstances

Energy is transferred from the mains supply by an electric current to the lamps. Each coulomb of charge that moves through the connecting wires carries a certain amount of energy, related to the potential difference of the mains supply.

If the battery is not fully charged, some of the energy transferred by the electric current is transferred to and stored in the battery unit.

Energy transferred to the lamps by the electric current is then transferred to the surroundings as light. Energy is also dissipated by heating; this increases the thermal energy store of the surrounding air.

During a power cut

Energy is transferred from the store in the battery by an electric current to the lamps. The charge that moves through the wires carries a certain amount of energy, related to the potential difference across the battery terminals. The lamps transfer energy as light waves to the surroundings and the hot lamp transfers energy to the surroundings by heating the air.
sets.partialHtml:
11 Under normal circumstances, energy is transferred from mains by the electricity flowing through the wires. The lights change the energy transferred by the electricity into stored heat energy. The stored heat energy is transferred to the air by light and heating.

When there is a power cut, the chemical energy stored inside the battery unit is transferred by electricity to the lights where it is stored as heat energy. The stored heat energy is then transferred to the air by light and heating.

This answer is rather confused. The student obviously does not fully understand the concepts associated with energy stores and transfers. The answer has identified energy stored as heat (internal/thermal) in the lights which is then transferred to the air (surroundings) by light (radiation) and heating. The answer has not explained clearly how the energy is transferred by electrical work, and it has missed how it is stored in the battery unit.

Some of the reasoning is correct and there are some logical links between the statements, so this is a Level 2 answer. Four of the indicative content statements have been partially met as the word ‘heat’ has been used instead of internal or thermal. This means that the answer is not fully clear, and therefore, Level 2.

3 out of 6 marks awarded.

Figure 5

Fool’s gold (iron pyrite)

Density = 5.0 g/cm3

Pure gold

Density = 19.3 g/cm3

A simple way to tell the difference between a sample of fool’s gold and pure gold is to measure the density of a sample of each.

Describe a method to identify each sample.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:

Answers

Mark

AO/

12

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Density requires the measurement of a mass and a volume.

The mass of each sample can be measured using an electronic balance.

Pour water into a displacement / eureka can until…

the water is the same level as the spout.

Carefully put a sample into the water, avoiding splashing.

Collect the displaced water in a measuring cylinder.

Measure and record the volume of water displaced by the sample.

Repeat for the second sample.

Or

Select a measuring cylinder that the nugget will fit inside.

Half fill the measuring cylinder with water.

Measure and record the initial volume.

Carefully place the nugget in the water.

Measure and record the final volume.

The volume of the object equals (final volume − initial volume).

Repeat for the second sample.

density=massvolume

Compare each density. The fool’s gold sample will have a density of approximately 5 g/cm3 and the gold sample will have a density of approximately 19.3 g/cm3.
sets.modelHtml:
12 Measure the mass of the first sample using an electronic balance.

Put an empty beaker under the spout of a displacement can.

Use another beaker to pour water into the displacement can until water comes out of the spout.

When the water has stopped dripping, place an empty measuring cylinder under the spout.

Carefully lower the sample into the displacement can so that it is completely submerged.

Collect and record the volume of all the water that comes out of the spout into the
measuring cylinder.

The volume of water displaced equals the volume of the sample.

Calculate density using density= massvolume.

Repeat for the second sample.

The sample with the higher density is pure gold.

sets.questionHtml:
14 A plastic canister can be made to ‘explode’ by placing half an antacid tablet (mostly calcium carbonate) into the canister with a small amount of hydrochloric acid inside it. The canister lid is pushed on and the canister is turned upside down. After a few seconds, the canister flies off as shown in Figure 7.

Figure 7

The calcium carbonate in the antacid tablet reacts with the hydrochloric acid to produce carbon dioxide gas.

Explain, in terms of particles and pressure, why the canister explodes and flies off.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
14 A plastic canister can be made to ‘explode’ by placing half an antacid tablet (mostly calcium carbonate) into the canister with a small amount of hydrochloric acid inside it. The canister lid is pushed on and the canister is turned upside down. After a few seconds, the canister flies off as shown in Figure 7.

Figure 7

The calcium carbonate in the antacid tablet reacts with the hydrochloric acid to produce carbon dioxide gas.

Explain, in terms of particles and pressure, why the canister explodes and flies off.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref.

14

Level 3: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, given in detail and logically linked to form a clear account

5–6

AO1

4.4.1.2

Level 2: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, and there are attempts at logically linking. The resulting account is not fully clear.

3–4

Level 1: Points are identified and stated simply, but their relevance is not clear and there is no attempt at logical linking.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

The chemical reaction produces carbon dioxide gas inside the canister.

The carbon dioxide mixes with the air inside the canister.

The gas particles hit the inside surface area of the canister with a force, exerting a pressure.

As more carbon dioxide gas particles are produced by the chemical reaction, the pressure inside the canister increases…

…because the number of collisions per second between the gas and the canister walls increases.

Eventually, the force exerted on the inside of the canister is greater than the force of friction holding the lid to the canister.

This causes the body of the canister to move upwards away from the lid.

OR

Explanation involving rate of change of momentum of escaping gas exerts an upwards force.
sets.modelHtml:
14 When carbon dioxide is produced in the reaction the particles are now in a gas and not in a solid or liquid.

The particles in a gas are moving much faster than the particles of a solid or liquid and they are free to move around in the container. When they hit the walls of the container they exert a pressure. There is pressure outwards on the sides, upwards on the top and also downwards on the lid.

As more carbon dioxide is produced, the particles hit the walls more frequently so there is an increase in pressure.

Eventually the total force of the gas upwards on the area of the lid is greater than the contact force between the lid and the canister, so the canister explodes upwards.
sets.partialHtml:
14 Carbon dioxide gas is produced by the reaction inside the canister.

The particles of gas exert a pressure on the canister because as they move around inside the canister they hit the inside walls with a force.

More carbon dioxide is produced and the pressure increases.

When the pressure gets too big then the canister breaks away from the lid and it goes up.

Some of the relevant points listed in the Indicative content are made (Level 1), but the link between force and gas pressure is not made clear. There is some logical thinking as the sequencing of the explanation is correct (Level 2) but it is not clear how the lid and the canister break apart. This means that the answer just goes into Level 2.

3 out of 6 marks awarded.

Indicative content

Similarities:

(Both isotopes) have the same number of protons.

(Both isotopes) have the same number of electrons.

The periodic table symbol has the same number (17) of protons (and electrons) as both of the isotopes.

Differences:

Chlorine-35 has 18 neutrons and chlorine-37 has
20 neutrons.

Chlorine-37 has 2 more neutrons than chlorine-35 / (both of the isotopes) have different numbers of neutrons.

Reason for mass = 35.5:

The symbol on the periodic table has a mass number of 35.5 because of the percentages found in nature are different.

There is more (75%) chlorine-35 found in nature than chlorine-37 (25%), so the overall atomic mass is closer to 35 than 37.

15.2 Chlorine-35 has 17 protons, 17 electrons and 18 neutrons. Chlorine-37 has the same number of protons and the same number of electrons but has 2 more neutrons.

16 The Turin Shroud is a piece of cloth that some people claim was the cloth that Jesus Christ’s body was wrapped in following his crucifixion. The cloth appears to show a faint imprint of a man with similar injuries to those suffered by Jesus during his death (Figure 8).

Here is some information about the Turin Shroud
taken from the internet.

Image of the
Turin Shroud

The first written account of the shroud was recorded in medieval times by a bishop who identified it as a forgery and claimed that an unnamed artist had confessed to producing it.

Jesus died between AD 30 and AD 33.

In 1988, a small fragment of the shroud was radiocarbon dated by three independent laboratories: Tucson (USA), Oxford (UK) and Zurich (Switzerland).

The shroud fragment was taken from one place on the edge of the shroud and divided into three pieces. One for each laboratory.

The three laboratories used a similar carbon dating technique and published the following results:

Laboratory

Tucson

Oxford

Zurich

Age (years)

646

750

676

Uncertainty (years)

31

30

24

Critics of the radiocarbon dating analysis point out that:

the sample was taken from one place on the edge of the cloth, which may have been repaired in medieval times

the shroud was damaged by a fire in 1532

many thousands of people have handled the shroud over the course of its lifetime.

Figure 8

Use the information supplied on the previous page, as well as other knowledge and understanding to evaluate the evidence for and against the Turin Shroud being a
medieval forgery.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref.

16

Level 3: A judgement, strongly linked and logically supported by a sufficient range of correct reasons, is given.

5–6

AO1

4.4.1.2

Level 2: Some logically linked reasons are given. There may also be a simple judgement.

3–4

Level 1: Relevant points are made. They are not logically linked.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

A judgement (for or against the shroud being a medieval forgery) should be made, with evidence for AND against considered.

For the shroud being a medieval forgery:

The radiocarbon dates range from 646 to 750 years old. This gives a possible date range of 1238 AD to 1342 AD.

The medieval bishop first mentioned this artefact in 1390 AD – this date is within the range given by the radiocarbon dates.

The radiocarbon dates were reproducible by the three different laboratories.

The range of uncertainties produced by the three different laboratories were very close together. The percentage uncertainties are very similar: 4.8%; 4.0% and 3.6%. This means that the measurements are very repeatable.

Against the shroud being a medieval forgery:

The tests were not blind tests.

The sample may have been contaminated by the many different environments it has been kept in since being produced.

The sample used may have been a piece of medieval cloth used to repair the shroud.

The fire in 1532 may have damaged the shroud, or contaminated it with much later fibres from other medieval garments.
sets.modelHtml:
16 On balance, I think the Turin shroud is a medieval forgery.

Three laboratories have independently used the same technique (radiocarbon dating) on the cloth to give similar results:

Ages: 1988 − 646 = 1342(±31); 1988 − 750 = 1238(±30); 1988 − 676 = 1312(±24)

All these are in the 14th or 13th centuries, and not from the time of Jesus’s death around 2000 years ago.

Percentage uncertainty Tucson = (31 ÷ 646) × 100% = 5%

All the results have a low percentage uncertainty and even the maximum possible ages are still within the medieval period.

The dates all agree with the date of the first mention of the shroud in history, which says that it was a forgery and quoted a confession.

Arguments against the shroud being a medieval forgery are that the shroud may have been repaired in medieval times so the results could be from the cloth used for repair. Handling the shroud could have contaminated it with dirt so the results could be the age of modern dirt. The tests did not involve the whole shroud, only a very small area so there may be older areas than the piece tested. Damage from the fire could have affected the validity of the carbon dating method.
sets.partialHtml:
16 I think that the Turin Shroud is a medieval forgery. The reason why I think this is because the radiocarbon dates given have a mean age of 691 years so a date of 1297 AD. This is earlier than the first recorded account of the shroud at 1390 AD. The forger could have used an old piece of cloth to fool the people at the time. Modern science has been able to date the cloth in the shroud quite accurately.

The radiocarbon tests were carried out by three independent laboratories so they are reproducible because they all used a similar method and got similar results.

I don’t think smoke would change the type of cloth used and even if the cloth was contaminated with later fibres it would still produce a date of about 1297 AD.

The only piece of evidence that could be questioned is that the sample was only taken from one part of the shroud and that could be a medieval repair. There would still be AD 30 to AD 33 fibres in the sample.

The student has made a positive judgement and has used the evidence to clearly back up their answer. This is clearly Level 3. They have used a range of the available ‘for’ evidence and they have included (a correct) mean calculation of the age and date of the shroud, also Level 3. They have only partially considered the ‘against’ evidence, hence only 5, not 6.

5 out of 6 marks awarded.

This is inserted directly into the tumour as a tiny solid ‘seed’ which is kept inside the tumour for about 2 weeks, during which the radiation kills the cancerous cells of the tumour. Mark

AO/

17

Level 2: Scientifically relevant features are identified; the way(s) in which they are similar/different is made clear and (where appropriate) the magnitude of the similarity/difference is noted.

No relevant content

Indicative content

Procedure 1:

Radium-223 is not appropriate as it is an alpha emitter, and all the alpha particles would be absorbed by the body tissue and would not escape the body.

Nitrogen-14 and iridium-192 are both beta emitters so the beta particles would be mostly absorbed by the breast tissue and so would not form a very clear image. These two are also not suitable.

The two gamma emitters, technetium-99 and iodine-123, would be most suitable for this procedure, because the gamma rays would escape the body and form a good image in the camera.

Technecium-99 would be the best radioisotope to choose, because in order to reduce the radioactive dose, a short half-life is preferred.

A half-life of 6 hours would be enough for blood to fully flow through the body, but would be safe after about 30 hours
(5 half-lives).

Procedure 2:

Radium-223 is not appropriate, as it is an alpha emitter and all the alpha particles would be absorbed by the body tissue immediately around the ‘seed’ and would not penetrate into the edges of the tumour.

The two gamma emitters, technetium-99 and iodine-123, are not suitable because the gamma rays would not be absorbed by the tumour and would escape the body.

Both the beta emitters, nitrogen-14 and iridium-192, could be suitable as the beta particles would be absorbed fully by all parts of the tumour.

Nitrogen-14 would not be suitable because the half-life is too short. The radiation would have dropped to background levels after about 50 minutes.

Iridium-192 would be the best choice because it would stay radioactive for the full 14 days of treatment.
sets.modelHtml:
17 Two isotopes are beta emitters (nitrogen-14 and iridium-192), two are gamma emitters (technetium-99 and iodine-123), and radium-223 is an alpha emitter.

Three have very short half-lives of minutes (nitrogen-14) to hours (technetium-99 and iodine-123) but two have half-lives of days (radium-223) and the longest half-life from (iridium-192).

In procedure 1 the isotope is inside and the camera is outside the body, so the radiation must penetrate flesh and bone. Alpha emitters would not be suitable as they are not very penetrating. Beta particles are more penetrating but would be mostly stopped. The isotope also remains inside the body so it should have as short a half-life as possible to minimise damage to the surrounding tissue. This means technetium-99 is best.

In procedure 2 to kill cancerous cells the radiation must pass through up to 1 cm of tissue, so alpha emitters are not suitable as too easily absorbed. The radiation must be absorbed inside the body so the gamma emitters are not suitable as the radiation passes straight through. The activity needs to stay high for 2 weeks to maximise the effectiveness of the treatment, so of the two beta emitters iridium-192 is best.

sets.questionHtml:
18 Future long-term manned space missions will require a reliable source of energy. Three systems have been used in the past.

(a) Solar panels are large areas of photovoltaic solar cells that convert sunlight directly into electrical energy. Solar panels are usually mounted on arrays (like ‘wings’) that can be deployed once the spacecraft is in space. The International Space Station uses four sets of panels, and they generate a combined power of 240 kW and have a combined area of
2500 m2. Solar panels cannot be used beyond the orbit of Jupiter because the solar radiation intensity is too weak. Solar panels need to be monitored continuously to ensure that they are facing in the direction of the Sun, but they only require minimal maintenance.

(b) Radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) are small compact electric generators that convert the heat released by the radioactive decay of an isotope directly into electrical energy. RTGs are a common power supply used on unmanned space probes, particularly those that travel far from the Sun, where solar panels are ineffective. RTGs are relatively safe, maintenance free, resilient under extreme conditions and long-lasting (decades). There is no chain reaction and they can provide approximately 6 kW of fixed power output. RTGs require very little monitoring.

(c) The Soviet Union used a small nuclear reactor called the BES-5 in a whole series of space probes from 1967 to 1988. The BES-5 was a true miniature nuclear reactor containing fuel rods, moderators and control rods. The heat that is generated from the controlled chain reaction is converted to electrical energy by a thermoelectric converter. BES-5 reactors are larger and more complex than RTGs and require constant monitoring and some routine maintenance. They can generate up to 100 kW of electrical power, and the power output can be varied according to need.

Evaluate the potential for these three systems as possible power solutions for a manned mission to Mars. The flight time to Mars is approximately 7 months and it is expected that the crew would stay on Mars for a few weeks. You need to consider systems suitable for the spacecraft and the Mars base.

[6 marks]

Indicative content

A judgement should be made as to which power systems to use.

The reasons for the choice should be made.

All three systems should be considered.

Solar panels

Non-hazardous to humans

Reliable power source if always pointing in the direction of the Sun

High power generation from a large array

Low maintenance

RTGs

Radiation hazardous to humans; shielding required

Reliable

Maintenance free

Require no monitoring

Good power output

Compact

Long lasting

BES-5 nuclear reactor

Radiation hazardous to humans; shielding required

Requires routine maintenance

Requires monitoring

High power output

Variable power output

Larger than RTGs

Choice

It is likely that any manned missions to Mars would use a combination of all three methods of power generation.

Spacecraft would probably use solar panels, as Mars is closer to the Sun than Jupiter. Large area solar panels could provide similar power outputs to the ISS.

Spacecraft would also use a small nuclear reactor like the BES-5 to provide a variable higher power output for life-support systems. This would need shielding to protect the crew.

On the surface of Mars, it is likely that a combination of solar panels and RTGs would be used. RTGs are more compact, reliable and require much less monitoring than nuclear reactors. The power requirements on the surface of Mars are likely to be less than that needed by the spacecraft. RTGs could be placed away from the crew pods on the surface, keeping them safe. RTGs would be needed to produce energy at night and during sandstorms.
sets.modelHtml:
18 Solar panels are suitable as the Sun will be visible throughout the journey and Mars is not as distant as Jupiter, so the solar radiation intensity will be enough. Solar panels are easy for the crew to maintain and not hazardous. The power output is the highest.

Solar panels are less suitable for the surface of Mars, because during the night the panels will be in darkness and not generate any power. The direction of panels would also need to be continually adjusted during the day to get maximum power depending on the angle of the Sun’s rays. However, the power requirements on the surface of Mars would be less, as there is no power needed, e.g. for thrusters to adjust course.

RTGs produce power continuously and don’t need maintaining so would be good on voyage and also on Mars. However, like the BES-5, they produce ionising radiation which could harm the crew, so precautions would be needed. The power output is also the lowest.

The BES-5 is potentially the most hazardous due to the chain reaction, which needs monitoring to keep the reactor safe, and regular maintenance. However, the control rods can be used to stop the chain reaction. This also means that the power output can be reduced – or increased, if not enough power was generated from the other sources, e.g. at night.

I think that a manned space mission to Mars would use all three methods, using mainly solar on the journey and more use of the variable BES-5 on Mars.
sets.partialHtml:
18 I think that a manned space mission to Mars would use solar panels and RTGs.

Mars is closer to the Sun than Jupiter so solar panels can be used. These will provide enough power for life support systems like on the International Space Station. These could be used on the spacecraft to and from Mars and on any Mars base. Solar panels are not radioactive, so they are not hazardous to the crew. The panels are also reliable and require little maintenance.

On the surface of Mars, the base would need solar panels and RTGs. The solar panels could provide the main power requirements, but RTGs would be needed at night or during times when the Sun is obscured by a storm.

The students answer evaluates two out of the three systems suggested so cannot access Level 3 as it does not show a sufficient range of reasons. A judgement is given, and the reasons given are included in the indicative content. This means that the answer is in Level 2. The judgments and reasons are linked.

4 out of 6 marks awarded.

Extra apparatus needed:

Clamp, stand and boss

6 × 1 N slotted weights

Ruler with mm scale

Reducing systematic error:

Reduce zero error by ensuring pointer is set to zero before adding each set of weights.

Method

Support the newtonmeter using a stand, boss and clamp.

Zero the pointer on the newton scale, using the zero
adjust knob.

Add a 1 N weight.

Measure and record movement of the pointer (equal to the extension of the spring).

Remove the weight and check zero offset, adjust to zero
if required.

Repeat for 2, 3, 4 and 5 N.

Repeat for 6 N but check if the pointer is off the scale;
if so, ignore.
sets.modelHtml:
20 Hang the newtonmeter from a rod clamped to a retort stand.

With no weights attached to the newtonmeter, align your eye with the pointer scale to ensure no parallax error.

Use the zero adjust knob to adjust the position of the pointer until it is aligned with the 0 on the scale. This removes the zero error (systematic error).

Add a 1 N weight to the hook and record the new position of the pointer; again, align your eye with the pointer. This is the extension of the newtonmeter.

Remove the weight and check there is no zero offset. The spring should not be permanently stretched, but a small adjustment may be needed.

Hang two 1 N weights on the hook. Measure the new extension.

Add a third, fourth and fifth 1 N weight to the hook. Each time you add a weight, measure the new extension and check the zero when no weight is on the hook.

When the total weight is 6 N, check carefully to see if the pointer is off the scale and don’t use this pair of values.

Add a third, fourth and fifth 1 N weight to the hook. Each time you add a weight, measure the new extension and check the zero when no weight is on the hook.

When the total weight is 6 N, check carefully to see if the pointer is off the scale and don’t use this pair of values.

21 When scuba diving using compressed air, if the depth and pressure become too great, then the oxygen in the compressed air becomes toxic. This affects the central nervous system and the diver will black out and start having convulsions.

Air pressure on the surface is 101 325 Pa (or 1 atmosphere, atm); 80% of this is due to the nitrogen gas in the air and 20 % is due to the oxygen gas, so the partial pressure due to the oxygen (ppO2) is 0.2 atm.

Oxygen becomes toxic at a partial pressure of 1.4 atm.

21.1 Calculate the air pressure, in Pa, when the oxygen partial pressure is 1.4 atm.

[2 marks]

Air pressure (when ppO2 = 1.4 atm) = Pa

21.2 Use your answer to 03.1 to calculate the depth of seawater where the oxygen in the inhaled air of a diver becomes toxic.

Density of seawater = 1029 kg/m3

Gravitational field strength = 9.8 N/kg

[4 marks]

Depth = m

22 Figure 11 shows some of the apparatus needed to perform an experiment to investigate the effect of varying the mass of an object on the acceleration produced by a constant force. A datalogger is used to automatically record measurements and it is programmed to measure the acceleration of the trolley directly when the double interrupt card passes through the light-gate.

Figure 11

Method

1. Set up the apparatus as shown in Figure 11. Ensure there is a 1 N weight on the hanger.

2. Turn on the datalogger.

3. Allow the weight to fall, and measure and record the acceleration of the trolley through the light-gate.

4. Reset the experiment and add 1 N to the hanger, so that there is a total of 2 N.

5. Repeat steps 3 and 4 for a total of 3, 4 and 5 N.

The experimental set-up and method described above is incorrect. Identify the errors and plan a correct method, including any extra apparatus required.

[6 marks]

The experimental set-up and method described above is incorrect. Identify the errors and plan a correct method, including any extra apparatus required.

[6 marks]

Indicative content

Method errors

This experiment will (incorrectly) investigate the effect of varying the force on the acceleration of the trolley.

The experiment does not control the mass of the object.

The experiment should have:

Independent variable = mass of trolley

Dependent variable = acceleration of trolley

Control variable = weight on the slotted hanger

Extra apparatus needed

Electronic balance

Correct Method

Add 2 N to the slotted weight hanger.

Measure and record the mass of the trolley, string and
2 N slotted weights and hanger.

Set up the apparatus as shown in the diagram.

Turn on the datalogger.

Allow the weight to fall, and measure and record the acceleration of the trolley through the light-gate.

Reset the experiment and add 0.2 kg mass to the trolley.

Repeat steps 3 and 4 for 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1.0 kg added mass.
sets.modelHtml:
22 In steps 3 and 5, the wrong variable is altered. The force used to accelerate the trolley should be constant, so the experiment should always be done with just 1 N attached to the string over the pulley. This is the controlled variable. The variable being investigated is the mass of an object being accelerated, and this has not been measured.

Correct method:

First use an electronic balance to measure the mass of the trolley, string and hanger with 1 N slotted weight. This is M.

Measure the acceleration of this system using the method described in steps 1 to 3.

Place a 100 g mass on top of the trolley. Do not change the weight on the string. The total mass being accelerated is now M + 100 g.

Measure the acceleration when the hanging weight is released. Take multiple readings to calculate a mean.

Place another 100 g mass on top of the trolley and measure the acceleration for the total mass of M + 200 g.

Continue till there are at least 5 pairs of measurements for mass and acceleration.
sets.partialHtml:
22 I don’t think that this experiment will work because its varying the wrong thing.

The independent variable should be the mass of the trolley and the dependent variable is the acceleration. The weight on the hanger is the control variable and should be constant each time.

In order to do this properly you should:

Set up the experiment as shown in the diagram.

Allow the weight to fall and measure and record the acceleration of the trolley.

Add 100 g to the trolley and repeat step 2

Repeat for 200, 300, 400 and 500 g added masses.

The student’s answer correctly identifies that the experiment is investigating the incorrect variables and has identified the correct ones. The experiment will lead to a valid outcome so is clearly in Level 3. However, the student’s answer does not include measuring and recording the mass of the trolley, string and hanger and does not suggest using a balance to measure the masses.

5 out of 6 marks awarded.

parts.html:

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Extra information

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref.

23

Principle of conservation of momentum

Total momentum before the collision = total momentum after the collision

Before collision:

Momentum of A

= mass of A × velocity of A

=1200 × 1.5 = 1800 kg m/s

Momentum of B = 0 (the wagon is not moving)

Total momentum before collision = 1800 + 0 = 1800 kg m/s

After collision:

Momentum of A + B

= (mass of A + mass of B) × v

= (2800 v) kg m/s

1800 = 2800 v

v=18002800

=0.64 m/s

This can be implied later.

A value of 0.64 m/s scores 6 marks.

24 In the air, on Earth, a hammer and a feather dropped at the same time will not reach the ground at the same time (Figure 21). However, in a vacuum such as on the Moon, the hammer and feather will both touch the ground at the same time. This was proved in a famous experiment carried out by astronaut Dave Scott during the Apollo 15 moon landing in 1971.

Figure 21

Explain why the hammer hits the ground first on Earth, but both the hammer and the feather hit the ground at the same time on the Moon.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
24 In the air, on Earth, a hammer and a feather dropped at the same time will not reach the ground at the same time (Figure 21). However, in a vacuum such as on the Moon, the hammer and feather will both touch the ground at the same time. This was proved in a famous experiment carried out by astronaut Dave Scott during the Apollo 15 moon landing in 1971.

Figure 21

Explain why the hammer hits the ground first on Earth, but both the hammer and the feather hit the ground at the same time on the Moon.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref.

24

Level 3: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, given in detail and logically linked to form a clear account.

5–6

AO1

4.3.3

4.5.1.3

4.5.6.1.5

Level 2: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, and there are attempts at logically linking. The resulting account is not fully clear.

3–4

Level 1: Points are identified and stated simply, but their relevance is not clear and there is no attempt at logical linking.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Objects fall due to the action of gravity on their mass.

They fall at the same rate if gravity is the only force acting on the objects.

On Earth:

In air there is air resistance/friction acting on the objects.

Air resistance acts in the opposite direction to the force of gravity acting on the falling object.

Air resistance depends upon the area of the object.

Feathers have a low weight but a high surface area, so the air resistance is a similar size to the feather’s weight.

Hammers have a low surface area, so they have a low air resistance compared to their weight.

Hammers fall at a higher rate than feathers through air on Earth.

On the Moon:

There is no air, so there is no air resistance.

Both objects fall at the same rate and hit the ground at the same time.
sets.modelHtml:
24 The hammer and the feather fall because there is a resultant force downwards. The resultant force is equal to the weight minus the air resistance.

Acceleration of an object is given by a = resultant force/mass and if there is no air resistance
a = weight/mass = mg/m, so acceleration only depends on the gravitational field strength g of the planet.

This is why on the Moon, which has no air and so no air resistance, both hammer and feather fall at the same rate and both touch the ground at the same time.

On the Earth there is air resistance. The size of the force from air resistance depends on the surface area of the object. A feather has a large surface area, so even though the feather’s weight is very small, air resistance is similar in size to weight and the acceleration is very low. For the hammer, the weight is much larger than air resistance, so the acceleration is hardly affected. The hammer hits the ground much sooner than the feather.
sets.partialHtml:
24 On Earth there is air resistance, and this depends on the surface area of the object that is falling. Feathers have a big surface area, so they have a big air resistance which causes them to fall slowly. The hammer has a small surface area, so it has a small air resistance, so it falls fast.

On the Moon, there is no air so there is no air resistance. This means that they both fall at the same rate.

The students answer does not explain why objects fall. It does explain how on Earth, in air, air resistance depends upon the surface area of the object. There is no reference to air resistance opposing the falling motion of the objects. The ideas of air resistance and surface area are identified and linked as is the fact that on the Moon, objects fall at the same rate due to the lack of air resistance. This means it is at Level 2. The answer is not clear enough as the link between the action of gravity (weight) and air resistance is not explained so it cannot get
Level 3.

3 out of 6 marks awarded.

25 A student sets-up a ripple tank to determine the speed of water waves in the tank as shown in Figure 13. He uses the camera on his mobile phone to take a picture of the waves and the metre ruler on the white card under the ripple tank.

Figure 13

Evaluate the suitability of this method for determining the speed of the water waves in the tank.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
25 A student sets-up a ripple tank to determine the speed of water waves in the tank as shown in Figure 13. He uses the camera on his mobile phone to take a picture of the waves and the metre ruler on the white card under the ripple tank.

Figure 13

Evaluate the suitability of this method for determining the speed of the water waves in the tank.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref.

25

Level 3: A judgement, strongly linked and logically supported by a sufficient range of correct reasons, is given.

5–6

AO3

4.6.1.2

WS 2.3, 2.7

Level 2: Some logically linked reasons are given. There may also be a simple judgement

3–4

Level 1: Relevant points are made. They are not logically linked.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

A judgement should be made, about the suitability of this method for determining the speed of water waves in the tank.

The method could be used to determine the speed of the water waves, however, it does not measure the frequency of the waves.

The method will be able to measure the wavelength of the waves.

The distance occupied by 10 waves can be measured from the photo taken by the mobile phone using the ruler as a scale.

The method would also need a measurement of the frequency of the waves, by counting the number of waves produced in 10 seconds (for example).

Wave speed = frequency × wavelength

OR

Need to measure the time taken for one wave to travel through the length of the ruler.

Wave speed = length of rulertime to travel down the ruler for one wave to travel the length of the ruler

Overall, this method is incomplete so will not measure the speed of the waves.
sets.modelHtml:
25 The method won’t work well because you need two measurements: distance travelled and time taken. Speed = distance travelledtime taken.

The method could be used to measure the distance travelled by one line of wave crests. You also need to film a stopwatch showing the time it took, e.g. to move between two marks on the paper 50 cm apart.

The camera angle is not directly above the pattern of the waves and the ruler. This means there will be an error measuring the distance moved by the wave crests.

The method does not mention taking repeats and finding a mean. Without changing the setting of the power supply, as this would change the frequency of the waves produced on the water surface, find the mean of several timings for the same distance.
sets.partialHtml:
25 I don’t think that this method will work very well because it needs to measure the frequency of the waves as well.

The equation that you need is:

wave speed = frequency × wavelength

The method shown will allow you to measure the wavelength because you could use the picture of the waves and the ruler to measure the distance needed for 10 waves and then divide this number by 10.

You could measure the frequency of the waves by counting how many are made in
10 s and then dividing that number by 10.

You could then use the equation to work out the wave speed.

This answer covers all the key indicative content and gives a judgement about how good the method is. It is in Level 3 as a judgement is made with sufficient correct reasons. The answer covers: what the method does well; how it does not measure frequency and includes how to measure the frequency. There is no critical evaluation of sources of error and how these could be reduced.

5 out of 6 marks awarded.

Place the semi-circular block in the middle of the white paper.

Draw around the outline of the block using a sharp pencil and then remove it from the paper.

Using the protractor, draw in a normal line either side of the flat (plane) face of the block, in the middle of face.

Use the protractor to mark in an incident beam at an angle of 30° to the normal.

Replace the semi-circular block on the white paper.

Turn on the raybox, select a single slit, and adjust the raybox until it produces a single narrow beam of light.

Manoeuvre the white paper into position so that the raybox beam travels down the 30° angle of incidence line.

Mark the position of the refracted beam using a sharp pencil.

Remove the block and complete the path of the refracted beam using a ruler.

Measure and record the angle of refraction.

Repeat the experiment twice more using clean sheets of white paper.

Calculate a mean angle of refraction.

To reduce uncertainties:

Make sure the beam is as narrow as possible.

Use a sharp pencil.

Repeat readings.

Calculate a mean value of the angle of refraction.

26 Draw around the block onto the paper, then remove the block and at a point in the middle of the flat line use a protractor and ruler to draw a line at 90° to this line.

Angle the ray box so that the ray of light enters the flat side of the glass block along the line at 30° to the normal.

Mark the refracted ray of light where it leaves the glass.

Remove the block and draw in the refracted ray with a ruler.

Use a protractor to measure the angle between the refracted ray and the normal.

Repeat the procedure 3 times and find the mean angle of refraction.

To minimise uncertainty in measuring the angle, use a sharp pencil and make sure the beam is as narrow as possible.

(The independent variable is the type of surface and the dependent variable is the intensity of the infra-red emitted as measured on the infrared detector).

The control variables are:

the temperature of the water inside the Leslie cube

the volume of water inside the Leslie cube

the distance of the infrared detector from the cube’s surface.

(the temperature of the surrounding air)

Method

Set-up the experiment as shown in the diagram but measure and record the distance of the infrared detector from the face of the Leslie cube using a ruler.

Fill up the Leslie cube up to the top, with hot water from a kettle.

Put a thermometer into the water and stir the water and allow to cool to a temperature of 90°C.

Measure and record the infrared intensity shown on the infrared detector.

Pour out the water from the Leslie cube. Turn the cube around so that the infrared detector is measuring a different face.

Ensure that the distance of the infrared detector is the same as in 1.

Repeat steps 2–6

Repeat for each face of the Leslie cube.

Repeat the experiment twice more for each face and then calculate a mean value of the infrared intensity for each face.

OR

Other slight variations of this are acceptable, provided that they show control of the volume and temperature of the water and the distance of the detector from the side of the Leslie cube and that the answer indicates that each face is tested.

A kettle, thermometer and ruler must be included in the answer.
sets.modelHtml:
27

Pour hot water from a kettle into the hole in the top of the cube, to fill the cube.

Position the sensor to point directly at the centre of one surface. Use a ruler to record the distance of the sensor from the cube.

Use a thermometer to measure the initial temperature of the water in the container. This should be the same (a control variable) for each surface investigated. If necessary, wait a short time for the water to cool to the same starting temperature each time.

At this starting temperature, record the reading on the infrared detector.

Carefully empty the cube and repeat procedure with a different side of the cube facing the sensor. Use the same volume of water as previously. Keep the distance between surface and sensor the same (a control variable) for each of the 4 surfaces investigated.

Repeat data collection so there are at least 3 measurements for each surface and calculate a mean.

Turn the Leslie cube around and measure the reading on the infrared detector. Do this for each face of the cube.

Repeat the experiment and calculate a mean average from each face of the cube.

sets.questionHtml:
30 A student wishes to sort some metal blocks that have come out of a school’s materials kit. The blocks all look similar, but the student has been told by the science technician that some blocks are made from aluminium; some are made from steel and the rest are permanent magnets. The technician has provided the student with a magnet, labelled with a north and south pole, for the task.

Design an experiment to identify each type of block.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
30 A student wishes to sort some metal blocks that have come out of a school’s materials kit. The blocks all look similar, but the student has been told by the science technician that some blocks are made from aluminium; some are made from steel and the rest are permanent magnets. The technician has provided the student with a magnet, labelled with a north and south pole, for the task.

Design an experiment to identify each type of block.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref.

30

Level 3: The method would lead to the production of a valid outcome. The key steps are identified and logically sequenced.

5–6

AO3

4.7.1.1

Level 2: The method would not necessarily lead to a valid outcome. Most steps are identified, but the method is not fully logically sequenced.

3–4

Level 1: The method plan would not lead to a valid outcome. Some relevant steps are identified, but links are not made clear.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Place the north pole of the magnet next to one of the metal blocks.

If the metal block is not attracted or repelled by the magnet then the block is made from aluminium.

If the block is attracted to the north pole of the magnet, then flip the test magnet over and hold the south pole next to the metal block.

If the metal block is also attracted to the south pole, then the block is made from steel.

If the block is repelled by the south pole of the magnet then the block is a permanent magnet.

Repeat for each block.

(Accept method based on starting with a south pole).
sets.modelHtml:
30 1. Use the magnet on the first metal block. If it is not attracted or repelled, the block is aluminium.

2. If the metal is attracted by the magnet, turn the magnet around to see if the metal is also attracted by the other pole. If it is, then the metal is steel.

3. If the block is attracted by one pole of the magnet, but repelled by the other, then the block is another magnet.

4. Repeat for each block.

If the block is attracted by one pole of the magnet, but repelled by the other, then the block is another magnet.

For a Level 3 answer, the method should lead to a valid outcome, which it will for any one block. The steps are logically sequenced (again Level 3), and all the key steps are identified except for repeating the method for all the blocks. 32 A student makes the simple electrical generator shown in Figure 18.

Figure 18

The student demonstrates this experiment to her class and states that it shows all the factors that affect the induced potential difference produced by the simple generator.

She varies the following quantities:

the magnetic flux density (by using a stronger magnet)

the number of turns of the coil

the direction of rotation of the magnet.

For each change that she makes, she highlights the movement of the needle on the voltmeter.

Evaluate this experiment as a demonstration of the generator effect.

[6 marks]
