Indicative content

The experiment will show most of the factors that affect the size of the induced potential difference – but not all.

It will show how the size (magnitude) of the induced potential difference will be increased by:

increasing the size of the magnetic flux density (by changing to a stronger magnet)

increasing the number of turns of the coil.

It will not show how increasing the speed of rotation of the magnet increases the size of the induced potential difference.

The experiment will show how the direction of the induced potential difference can be altered.

It will show how the direction of the induced potential difference depends upon the direction of rotation of the magnet.

increasing the strength of the magnet (increasing the magnetic flux density) increases the induced p.d.

increasing the number of turns on the coil increases the size of the induced p.d.

the direction of the induced potential difference can be altered by reversing the direction of rotation of the magnet.

One factor has not been demonstrated, however – that the induced p.d. increases if the magnet is moved faster.

The experiment shows how the size of the induced p.d. is increased by changing the strength of the magnet.

It also shows how increasing the number of turns on the coil also increases the size of the induced p.d.

The demonstration will also show how the direction of the induced p.d. changes, depending on the direction of rotation of the magnet.

sets.questionHtml:
34 Betelgeuse is a large red supergiant star in the constellation of Orion. It is believed to be a star that is close to becoming a supernova. If this happens, then the Betelgeuse supernova will become as bright as the full moon for about 30 days before fading over the following 400 days. Betelgeuse is about 20 times more massive than the Sun and will likely end its life as a neutron star.

Describe the stages in the life cycle of Betelgeuse, starting from its nebula, to its ultimate fate as a neutron star. For each stage describe the key features of the stage.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
34 Betelgeuse is a large red supergiant star in the constellation of Orion. It is believed to be a star that is close to becoming a supernova. If this happens, then the Betelgeuse supernova will become as bright as the full moon for about 30 days before fading over the following 400 days. Betelgeuse is about 20 times more massive than the Sun and will likely end its life as a neutron star.

Describe the stages in the life cycle of Betelgeuse, starting from its nebula, to its ultimate fate as a neutron star. For each stage describe the key features of the stage.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref.

34

Level 2: Scientifically relevant facts, events or processes are identified and given in detail to form an accurate account.

4–6

AO1

4.8.1.2

Level 1: Facts, events or processes are identified and simply stated but their relevance is not clear.

1–3

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Life cycle in order:

Nebula – cloud of interstellar gas and dust; the force of gravity pulls the particles of gas (and dust) together.

Protostar – a collapsed region of gas and dust heating up; not hot enough for nuclear fusion; when the temperature is hot enough nuclear fusion starts, so the star starts to shine.

Main sequence – star undergoing nuclear fusion of hydrogen to helium; the star is stable (not growing or shrinking) because the forces are balanced.

Red supergiant – star has reached the end of the main sequence stage (because it has run out of hydrogen /all the hydrogen fused to helium) and has expanded; very large star fusing elements heavier than hydrogen, so heavier elements (up to iron) are formed.

Supernova – massive explosion as the red supergiant collapses under its own gravity as nuclear fusion stops; outer layers (of the star) are blown away.

Neutron star – the very dense remnant of the red supergiant’s core – emitting huge amounts of radiation.
sets.modelHtml:
34 Betelgeuse formed from a nebula, which was gas and dust that came together because of gravitational attraction.

As the particles came together a protostar was created and the temperature of the particles increased.

When the temperature was high enough, nuclear fusion started and the star begin to shine.

In the main sequence stage the star was stable, and its size didn’t change. It carried on nuclear fusion of hydrogen to helium.

When all the hydrogen had fused to helium, the main sequence stage ended and the star expanded to a red supergiant. In this stage, heavier elements (up to iron) are produced by fusion.

Eventually nuclear fusion ended and the outer layers of the star blew away in a huge explosion – the supernova. This left a smaller, much denser core, which was the neutron star.
sets.partialHtml:
34 Betelgeuse formed from a nebula in space from gas and dust that came together because of gravity. The nebula must have been very big to form Betelgeuse, as it is 20 times more massive than the Sun.

It formed a main sequence star like the Sun, before swelling up to form the red supergiant. Eventually it will run out of fuel and explode as a supernova, which is a very big and bright explosion of the star, as bright as the full moon.

What’s left of Betelgeuse after the supernova will end up as a neutron star.

The student has identified five out of six of the key stages of Betelgeuse’s life cycle, although four were given in the question. The five stages given are in the correct order. They have given a number of relevant points but since the key features are not given for all the listed stages this is not a Level 2 answer.

3 out of 6 marks awarded.

sets.questionHtml:
35 A student creates the simple model of the expansion of the universe shown in Figure 19.

Figure 19

In the model. the rubber band represents the space of the universe shortly after the Big Bang. The star shapes represent the matter of the universe and the black line represents a gamma ray created at the time of the Big Bang. To model the expansion of the universe, the rubber band is slowly stretched.

Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of this model of the expansion of the universe.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
35 A student creates the simple model of the expansion of the universe shown in Figure 19.

Figure 19

In the model. the rubber band represents the space of the universe shortly after the Big Bang. The star shapes represent the matter of the universe and the black line represents a gamma ray created at the time of the Big Bang. To model the expansion of the universe, the rubber band is slowly stretched.

Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of this model of the expansion of the universe.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref.

35

Level 3: A judgement, strongly linked and logically supported by a sufficient range of correct reasons, is given.

5–6

AO3

4.8.2

Level 2: Some logically linked reasons are given. There may also be a simple judgement.

3–4

Level 1: Relevant points are made. They are not logically linked.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Overall – the student should give a judgment as to the overall effectiveness of the model of the expansion of the universe (e.g. good/bad because…).

Strengths

The model shows:

the space between the matter of the universe stretching out (expanding)

the increase in wavelength (red-shift) of radiation as the space in the universe expands – including reference to the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR)

that the rubber band can stretch at different rates at different times (as believed to be the case with the universe)

that far away galaxies move apart faster – star shapes closer to the ‘end’ of the band travel further in the same time (move faster) than the star shapes near the ‘middle’.

Weaknesses

The model does not show:

the expansion of the universe in three dimensions, as the rubber band only stretches along one axis (and actually gets narrower as it stretches) / only shows star shapes on the surface of the rubber band

that the Big Bang started at an infinitesimally small, very hot/dense point

that the universe is appearing to expand at an increasing rate, because the rubber band stretches quite easily at the start but gets increasingly more difficult to stretch as it gets longer.

The model incorrectly:

suggests there is a limit to how much the universe can expand.
sets.modelHtml:
35 The model is good because as the rubber is stretched all the star shapes move apart, showing how matter in the universe moves away from other matter.

The line for the gamma ray is also stretched out. This is like the observed light emitted from galaxies, which would increase in wavelength as the universe expands.

Another good point of the model is that the two outer star shapes move apart faster than the two inner star shapes. This is like more distant galaxies moving apart faster.

A weakness of the model is that it implies that matter in the universe itself is stretched, but particles such as electrons cannot be stretched, you can only increase the separation between particles.

Another weakness is that there is no ‘material’ (like the rubber band) that holds matter in the universe together. The rubber band will also only stretch to a maximum length, and may even break, but the universe can keep on expanding.
sets.partialHtml:
35 I think that the model is quite good because it shows the expansion of the universe. Its strengths are that as the rubber band is stretched, so the space between the stars gets bigger; this is what is happening in the universe. Also, as you stretch the rubber band, the length of the black line gets bigger. The line shows that the wavelength of the gamma rays gets bigger as the universe gets bigger. This is like the red-shift of the gamma rays into the cosmic microwave background.

Its weakness is that the rubber band only stretches in one direction as you pull it, whereas the universe expands in all directions.

Overall though, I think this is quite a good model and shows it well.

The student gives a judgement of some strengths and weaknesses, each supported with reasons. This is clearly Level 2. However, the points in the student’s answer do not have enough sufficient scientifically relevant features for a Level 3 answer.

This is a top Level 2 answer.

4 out of 6 marks awarded.

Some sodium chloride is found in layers of all rock called rock salt (Figure 1).

Plan an experiment to obtain pure solid sodium chloride from a sample of rock salt
in a school laboratory.

Include a reason for each of the steps in your method.

[6 marks]

parts.html:

sets.schemeHtml:

Mark

AO/

01

Level 3: The method would lead to the production of a valid outcome. The key steps are identified and logically sequenced.

5–6

AO3.3a

4.1.1.2 Chem, 5.1.1.2 CS WS 2.2, 2.3 AT4

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Crush the rock salt

With a mortar and pestle

To increase the surface area / make it easier to dissolve.

Add water to the rock salt in a beaker

To dissolve the salt / sodium chloride.

Warm the water

Stir the mixture

To make the salt / sodium chloride dissolve more quickly.

Filter

Using a funnel and filter paper

To remove the rock.

Collect the filtrate / sodium chloride solution in an evaporating basin.

Heat the solution

Until all of the water has evaporated.

Credit may be given for diagrams to illustrate the method.
sets.modelHtml: 01 I would crush the rock salt so that it is in smaller pieces and will dissolve more easily. I would do this using a mortar and pestle. I would tip the powder into a beaker and add water. I would warm the water by placing the beaker on a tripod and gauze and heating with a Bunsen burner and stir the mixture with a glass rod. This will help the salt to dissolve more quickly. After leaving the beaker to cool down, I would filter the mixture. The impurities will be left on the filter paper and the salt solution will collect in an evaporating basin. I would then heat the salt solution until all the water has evaporated.
sets.partialHtml:
01 I would crush the rock salt with a mortar and pestle. Then I would add water to the rock salt in a beaker and stir it. Filter it then heat the solution until all the water evaporates and just solid sodium chloride is left.

However, they have not included reasons for most of the steps in the method, so this is a Level 2 answer. They have given a correct reason for heating the solution, so the higher mark in Level 2 is awarded.

sets.modelHtml: 02 Both the plum pudding model and today’s model of an atom refer to an area of positive charge and negatively charged electrons in an atom. The protons have a positive charge and the neutrons are neutral. The plum pudding model assumes that the electrons are inside the ball of positive charge, like raisins in a pudding, whereas the modern model assumes that the electrons are moving around the nucleus in orbits.

Indicative content

The modern periodic table has elements arranged in order of increasing atomic number / number of protons.

Protons had not been discovered when Mendeleev published
his periodic table.

Argon atoms have a higher relative atomic mass than
potassium atoms as they have 18 protons and 22 neutrons.

Potassium atoms have 19 protons but (only) 20 neutrons.

Electronic structure provides additional evidence for the
different positions in the periodic table.

Argon has electronic structure 2.8.8.

There are electrons in three shells so it is in Period 3.

The outer shell is full of electrons so it is in Group 0.

Potassium has electronic structure 2.8.8.1.

There are electrons in four shells so it is in Period 4.

The outer shell has one electron so it is in Group 1.

Credit may be given for diagrams showing the electronic structures.
sets.modelHtml: 03 Mendeleev arranged the elements in order of increasing atomic mass. Elements are now arranged in the periodic table in order of increasing atomic number. The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom and protons had not been discovered when Mendeleev was working on the periodic table. Argon atoms have a mass number of 40 as they have 18 protons and 22 neutrons, but potassium atoms have a mass number of 39 as they have 19 protons and 20 neutrons. The electronic structures also show that argon should be before potassium. Argon atoms have 18 electrons arranged 2.8.8. There are three shells of electrons so it is placed in Period 3 and the outer shell has eight electrons so it is in group 0. Potassium atoms have 19 electrons arranged 2.8.8.1 so the four shells show that it is in Period 4 and the one electron in the outer shell shows it is in Group 1.
sets.partialHtml:
03 Elements are now arranged in the periodic table in order of increasing atomic number. Argon atoms have 18 protons so have atomic number 18 and potassium atoms have 19 protons and atomic number 19 so it comes after argon in the periodic table.

Also, argon atoms have the electronic structure 2.8.8 so it has full shells of electrons and is a noble gas in Group 0. Potassium atoms have the electronic structure 2.8.8.1 so it is in Group 1 as it has one electron in the outer shell. Argon atoms have three shells of electrons so it is in Period 3 and potassium atoms have four shells of electrons so it is in Period 4.

The student has given a detailed account including many relevant points about why argon is placed before potassium in the periodic table, so this is a Level 3 answer. However, they have not mentioned why argon has a higher relative atomic mass than potassium, so 5 marks are awarded rather than 6.

Methane has a low melting point because it has a simple molecular structure.

sets.modelHtml:
06 Methane consists of CH4 molecules with covalent bonds between the carbon atom and the hydrogen atoms.

These bonds are strong and difficult to break. There are only weak forces holding the molecules together, so methane has a low melting point as not much energy is needed to break these forces and separate the molecules. Methane does not conduct electricity as it does not have any ions or delocalised electrons to carry the current.

Diamond has a giant covalent structure with each carbon atom joined to four others in a lattice. All of these bonds are strong and difficult to break, so a lot of energy is needed to melt diamond and the melting point is high. Diamond does not conduct electricity as it does not have any ions or delocalised electrons.
sets.partialHtml:
06 Methane contains small molecules with covalent bonds between the atoms. Diamond is a giant structure with covalent bonds between the atoms. Not much energy is needed to break the covalent bonds in methane but a lot of energy is needed to break the bonds in diamond.

They don’t conduct electricity because they don’t contain ions or electrons.

The student has identified the types of structure (small molecules and giant) and that the (covalent) bonds in diamond need a lot of energy to break. They have also stated that they do not contain ions. However, they have omitted details about the bonding in methane and diamond (see the list in the indicative content), so this is a Level 2 answer. The statement that the covalent bonds in methane are broken when it melts is a common error in answers. It is important to remember that the covalent bonds between the atoms in the molecules are strong but that there are only weak forces between the molecules. It is the weak forces between the molecules that are overcome when methane melts. A Level 3 answer would show a clear understanding of which bonds or forces are broken when diamond and methane melt. It is incorrect to state that methane and diamond do not contain electrons. All substances contain electrons but there must be delocalised electrons to carry the current.

3 out of 6 marks awarded.

Similarities

Differences

Diagram of metallic bonding:

Whereas in magnesium chloride the magnesium ions each lose two electrons from their outer shell

sets.modelHtml:
07 Magnesium is a metal so has metallic bonding. Magnesium chloride has ionic bonding. Both of these types of bonding are strong and the particles are arranged in giant structures. In magnesium, the two electrons in the outer shell do not belong to any particular atom. They become delocalised and are free to move through the metal when it is connected to a supply of electricity. sets.questionHtml:
09 Some information about sunscreens and nanoparticles is given below.

Ultraviolet (UV) radiation is part of the natural radiation produced by the Sun. UVA radiation penetrates deeply into the skin and can cause premature ageing. UVB radiation is responsible for sunburn and plays a greater role in causing skin cancers than UVA.

There are two types of sunscreen.

Chemical absorbers (also called organic sunscreens) absorb UV radiation and stop it penetrating the skin. However, they can irritate the skin and cause allergies in
some people.

Physical blockers (or inorganic sunscreens) reflect and scatter UV radiation. They are generally considered safer than chemical absorbers, are better for sensitive skin and renowned for their broad-spectrum UV radiation-blocking abilities.

Zinc oxide and titanium dioxide are naturally white and used in physical blocking sunscreens. They provide strong sun protection, do not break down in sunlight and cause few health concerns. However, they leave a white, chalky film over the skin.

Since the 1980s, suncreens containing nanoparticles of zinc oxide and titanium dioxide have been used. The smaller the particles of zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, the better sun protection factor (SPF) but the worse the UVA protection. Sunscreens containing nanoparticles are transparent and rub into the skin easily.

Some studies indicate that large doses of nanoparticles can harm living cells and organs. A large number of studies show no evidence that these nanoparticles can cross the skin in significant amounts. Powdered titanium dioxide has been shown to cause lung cancer when inhaled by rats.

[Information based on www.choice.com.au/health-and-body/beauty-and-personal-care/skin-care-and-cosmetics/articles/sunscreen-and-nanoparticles and www.skincancer.org/risk-factors/uv-radiation/

Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the different types of sunscreen.

[6 marks]

Indicative content

Sunscreens are essential to prevent premature ageing and skin cancer.

Physical blockers are better than chemical absorbers because chemical absorbers may irritate the skin and cause allergies in some people.

Suncreens with nanoparticles are better than sunscreens without them because people are more likely to use them as they are easy to apply / rub into the skin

And don’t leave unsightly white marks on the skin.

However, as they cannot be seen, people may miss a bit of skin and that can burn in the sunlight.

They probably have less zinc oxide and titanium dioxide in them as their nanoparticles have a large surface area

So are more effective at reflecting the UV radiation.

However, the particle size must not be too small, so the UVA protection decreases too much.

There are some health concerns over the use of nanoparticles (in sunscreens).

There is no definite proof that long-term use of nanoparticles is completely safe but no proof that it is harmful either.

Sunscreens contain small amounts of nanoparticles and most people do not use them in large amounts.

The information about lung cancer in rats is not relevant

As people do not inhale sunscreens.
sets.modelHtml:
09 Sunscreens prevent people from getting skin cancer. Chemical absorbers stop the UV getting into the skin but some people cannot use them as they irritate the skin and cause allergies. Physical blockers are safer for sensitive skin and reflect the UV radiation. They have been used for a long time and don’t break down in sunlight.

Sunscreens with nanoparticles are clear and don’t leave any white marks, like the physical blockers, so are more attractive for people to use. However, it’s difficult to see if all the exposed skin has been covered and if people miss a bit, that area may burn. Some people are worried about using them but there is no proof whether they are harmful or safe and they do help to prevent skin cancer. Most people use sunscreens in small amounts when they are outside or on holiday. Those who work outside or live in countries with a lot of sunshine will use larger amounts so may have to be more careful. The information about powdered titanium dioxide causing lung cancer in rats is irrelevant as sunscreens are liquids so people don’t inhale any powder.

sets.questionHtml:
10 The law of conservation of mass states that no atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction. This means that the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants. A student carried out two experiments to investigate this law.

Experiment 1

The student found the mass of an ice cube in a beaker. They left the ice cube to melt and found the mass of the beaker and water. There was no change in mass.

Experiment 2

The student found the mass of a strip of magnesium ribbon in a crucible. They placed a lid on the crucible and heated it while lifting the lid a little from time to time. After cooling the crucible, the student found that the mass of crucible and contents had increased.

Explain why there was no change in mass during Experiment 1 but the mass increased during Experiment 2.

[6 marks]

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Experiment 1

This is a physical change / solid changes to liquid.

There is no change in the number of hydrogen and oxygen atoms.

There is no change in the number of (H2O) molecules in the ice and the water

As no new molecules are added and none are removed.

Therefore, the masses are the same and this confirms the law of conservation of mass.

Experiment 2

This is a chemical change.

Magnesium reacts with oxygen (from the air)

To form magnesium oxide.

2Mg + O2 → 2MgO

There are the same number of atoms of magnesium and oxygen on each side of the equation.

The student only weighs the magnesium and magnesium oxide.

Magnesium oxide is heavier than magnesium as it also contains oxygen.

The student could not weigh the oxygen from the air that reacted with the magnesium:

mass of magnesium + mass of oxygen = mass of magnesium oxide

So this also confirms the law of conservation of mass.

The student could determine the mass of oxygen:

mass of oxygen used = mass of magnesium oxide – mass of magnesium
sets.modelHtml:
10 When ice melts to form water a physical change occurs. All of the H2O molecules in solid ice stay as H2O molecules in liquid water, so nothing is added or removed. The mass stays the same so the law of conservation of mass is true. When magnesium is heated, it reacts with oxygen from the air to form magnesium oxide.

2Mg + O2 → 2MgO

This is a chemical reaction as a new product is formed. The balanced equation shows that there are two atoms of magnesium on each side and two atoms of oxygen on each side so no new atoms are added or taken away. So the law of conservation of mass is true. When the student carried out the experiment, she only weighed the magnesium at the start and the magnesium oxide at the end. She was unable to weigh the oxygen from the air. Using the law of conservation of mass, she could calculate the mass of oxygen used:

mass of oxygen = mass of magnesium oxide − mass of magnesium

A word or balanced equation for the reaction in Experiment 2 would have shown that magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide and help this student to gain a higher mark and move to the next level.

13 A student wrote the following plan for carrying out a titration using dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution.

Fill a burette with hydrochloric acid. Fill a pipette with the sodium hydroxide solution and empty it into a conical flask. Add 2 drops of universal indicator. Add the acid to the flask until the indicator changes colour. Note the burette reading.

Explain how this plan should be improved to carry out an accurate titration and obtain concordant results. Include reasons for the improvements.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
13 A student wrote the following plan for carrying out a titration using dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution.

Fill a burette with hydrochloric acid. Fill a pipette with the sodium hydroxide solution and empty it into a conical flask. Add 2 drops of universal indicator. Add the acid to the flask until the indicator changes colour. Note the burette reading.

Explain how this plan should be improved to carry out an accurate titration and obtain concordant results. Include reasons for the improvements.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref

13

Level 3: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, given in detail and logically linked to form a clear account.

5–6

AO3.3b

4.4.2.5 WS2.7 AT 1, 8

Level 2: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, and there are attempts at logically linking. The resulting account is not fully clear.

3–4

Level 1: Points are identified and stated simply, but their relevance is not clear and there is no attempt at logical linking.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Place a funnel in the burette to avoid spills when filling it.

Rinse the burette with hydrochloric acid before filling it to make sure there is no water / impurities.

Fill above the ‘0’ mark and acid let out of the tap to make sure the jet below the tap is full of acid.

Record the initial reading of acid in the burette.

Place a pipette filler on the pipette for safety.

Rinse the pipette with sodium hydroxide before filling it to the (graduation) mark.

Universal indicator is not suitable for a titration as it has too many different colours / does not show a clear colour change at the end point.

Use methyl orange/ phenolphthalein as indicator as they give a sharp colour change at the end point.

Place the conical flask on a white tile / piece of white paper so the colour change can be seen more easily.

Swirl the flask while adding the acid so the solutions mix well.

Add the acid dropwise / slowly near the end point to make sure that not too much is added.

Repeat the titration until 2 titres are obtained that are within 0.2 cm3 as these will be concordant.
sets.modelHtml:
13 The student should wear safety goggles and a lab coat and they should put a funnel in the top of the burette to avoid spilling any acid when filling it. They should rinse the burette with a little hydrochloric acid before filling it to make sure there is no water left in it. They should fill it above the ‘0’ mark and let acid out of the tap to make sure the part below the tap is full of acid. If there is an air bubble, the first reading will be wrong. They should record the initial reading of acid in the burette. They should place a pipette filler on the pipette for safety and rinse the pipette with sodium hydroxide before filling it to the mark. Then empty it into a conical flask and place it on a white tile. They should not use universal indicator, as it has too many different colours so it would be difficult to see the end point.

They could use methyl orange as indicator as it is yellow in sodium hydroxide, red in hydrochloric acid and orange when neutral. Add the acid slowly to the flask and swirl it.

When the indicator starts to change colour, add the acid dropwise to make sure that not too much is added. Record the volume of acid when the indicator just turns orange. The student should repeat the titration until 2 titres are obtained that are within 0.2 cm3 as these will be concordant.
sets.partialHtml:
13 The student should rinse the burette and pipette with the solutions they will be used to measure. They need to put a funnel in the top of the burette then fill it over the 0 mark, let some out and note the first reading. They need to use a pipette filler with the pipette. It’s better to use methyl orange as the indicator as it’s pink in acid, yellow in alkali and orange when neutral. Universal indicator has lots of different colours. Put the flask on a white tile and add the acid slowly until the indicator changes colour. Repeat the titration twice more.

This student has given a good description of most of the improvements that need to be made to carry out an accurate titration, so this is a Level 2 answer. Swirling the flask would also help the solutions to mix. Repeating the titration twice more would not necessarily give concordant results. For example, the titres could be 25.3, 24.8 and 24.3 cm3. These are not concordant as they are too far apart. In a titration, concordant titres should be within 0.2 cm3, for example 24.8 and 24.6 cm3. To achieve Level 3, the student should give more reasons for the improvements they have suggested as asked for in the question. The student has given a clear reason for not using universal indicator, so the higher mark in Level 2 is awarded.

4 out of 6 marks awarded.

14 The metals iron and aluminium occur in the Earth’s crust as ores containing iron oxide and aluminium oxide.

Iron is less reactive than carbon but aluminium is more reactive than carbon.

Iron and aluminium are extracted from their ores using different methods.

Explain why different methods are used to extract iron and aluminium from their ores.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
14 The metals iron and aluminium occur in the Earth’s crust as ores containing iron oxide and aluminium oxide.

Iron is less reactive than carbon but aluminium is more reactive than carbon.

Iron and aluminium are extracted from their ores using different methods.

Explain why different methods are used to extract iron and aluminium from their ores.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref

14

Level 3: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, given in detail and logically linked to form a clear account.

5–6

AO1.1

4.4.1.3, 4.4.3.3 Chem 5.4.1.3, 5.4.3.3 CS

Level 2: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, and there are attempts at logically linking. The resulting account is not fully clear.

Level 1: Points are identified and stated simply, but their relevance is not clear and there is no attempt at logical linking.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Iron is less reactive than aluminium / iron is lower in the reactivity series than aluminium.

Iron forms weaker bonds with oxygen than aluminium does with oxygen.

Iron oxide can be heated with carbon.

Carbon will remove the oxygen from iron oxide.

This is reduction.

Iron could be extracted by electrolysis.

But this is too expensive / uses too much energy.

Carbon is not reactive enough to remove the oxygen from aluminium oxide / aluminium oxide cannot be reduced by carbon.

Aluminium can only be extracted by electrolysis

Of molten aluminium oxide

Mixed with cryolite

To lower the melting point.

Aluminium is produced at the cathode.
sets.modelHtml:
14 Iron is extracted by heating iron oxide with carbon. The carbon takes the oxygen away from the iron oxide in a reduction reaction.

Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide mixed with cryolite. The cryolite lowers the melting point of aluminium oxide so less energy is needed to keep it molten. Aluminium is formed at the cathode. The aluminium ions gain electrons in a reduction reaction.

Different methods are used because iron is less reactive than aluminium. It could be extracted by electrolysis but that is more expensive. Carbon isn’t reactive enough to take the oxygen away from aluminium oxide, so electrolysis has to be used.
sets.partialHtml:
14 Iron is extracted by heating iron oxide with carbon. The carbon takes the oxygen away and leaves iron. Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis. The aluminium oxide must be heated until it is a liquid. Aluminium is formed at the anode.

The student has given some relevant points about the extraction of the two metals but they are not linked to explain why different methods are used, so this is a Level 1 answer. The higher mark is awarded as there are sufficient correct points. However, aluminium is formed at the cathode during electrolysis, not the anode. To achieve a higher mark, the student needs to explain why different methods are used to extract the metals. They should do this in terms of their positions in the reactivity series. The question states that iron is less reactive than carbon but aluminium is more reactive than carbon so the student should state that iron is less reactive than aluminium. It would also be helpful to include a few more facts about the extractions, as shown in the indicative content.

2 out of 6 marks awarded.

14 Iron is extracted by heating iron oxide with carbon. The carbon takes the oxygen away from the iron oxide in a reduction reaction.

Aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide mixed with cryolite. The cryolite lowers the melting point of aluminium oxide so less energy is needed to keep it molten. Aluminium is formed at the cathode. The aluminium ions gain electrons in a reduction reaction.

Different methods are used because iron is less reactive than aluminium. It could be extracted by electrolysis but that is more expensive. Carbon isn’t reactive enough to take the oxygen away from aluminium oxide, so electrolysis has to be used.

sets.modelHtml:
15 The results show that as the time doubles in experiments 1 and 2, the volumes of hydrogen and chlorine approximately double. There are small differences, but these could be due to experimental error. In these experiments the current is constant so the hypothesis that the volumes of hydrogen and chlorine are directly proportional to time is true.

In experiments 1 and 3, as the current increases by 1.5 the volumes of hydrogen and chlorine increase by approximately 1.5. In these experiments the time is constant so the hypothesis that the volumes of hydrogen and chlorine are directly proportional to the current is true.

The hypothesis that the volumes of hydrogen and chlorine are equal is not true as all three experiments show they are different. This hypothesis should be true as the balanced equation shows that 2 mol hydrochloric acid produces 1 mol hydrogen and 1 mol chlorine and equal moles of gas occupy equal volumes. The volume of chlorine is a lot lower than that of hydrogen in all the experiments so this cannot be caused by experimental error.

Chlorine is soluble in water so most of it dissolves as it travels up the tubes and less is collected than expected.
sets.partialHtml:
15 As the time doubles, the volume of hydrogen almost doubles and the volume of chlorine almost doubles, so this confirms the students’ hypothesis that the volumes are directly proportional to the time.

As the current increases from 0.4 to 0.6 amps, that is ×1.5. The volumes of hydrogen and chlorine also increase ×1.5, so this confirms the students’ hypothesis that the volumes are directly proportional to the current.

The volume of chlorine is much less than the volume of hydrogen. This could be caused by experimental error.

This student has correctly confirmed two of the students’ hypotheses, so this is a Level 2 answer, although it would have been better to refer to the experiment numbers they used to come to this conclusion or to state that the current or the time is constant, as appropriate. To achieve Level 3, the student would need to comment on why the students’ hypothesis that the volumes are equal is correct and give more detail on the difference between the volumes of hydrogen and chlorine collected.

3 out of 6 marks awarded.

16 A student wrote the following plan for carrying out an experiment for preparing pure, dry crystals of copper sulfate.

Pour some hydrochloric acid in a beaker. Add some copper oxide to the beaker and stir the mixture. Pour the solution into an evaporating basin. Heat the solution until all the water evaporates.

Explain how this plan should be improved to prepare a sample of pure, dry crystals of copper sulfate. Include reasons for the improvements.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
16 A student wrote the following plan for carrying out an experiment for preparing pure, dry crystals of copper sulfate.

Pour some hydrochloric acid in a beaker. Add some copper oxide to the beaker and stir the mixture. Pour the solution into an evaporating basin. Heat the solution until all the water evaporates.

Explain how this plan should be improved to prepare a sample of pure, dry crystals of copper sulfate. Include reasons for the improvements.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref

16

Level 3: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, given in detail and logically linked to form a clear account.

5–6

AO3.3b

4.4.2.2, 4.4.2.3 Chemistry 5.4.2.2, 5.4.2.3 Combined Science

Level 2: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, and there are attempts at logically linking. The resulting account is not fully clear.

3–4

Level 1: Points are identified and stated simply, but their relevance is not clear and there is no attempt at logical linking.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Hydrochloric acid would make copper chloride.

Use sulfuric acid instead

As that will make a sulfate.

The beaker of acid should be warmed

To increase the rate of reaction.

Add the copper oxide until there is some left on the bottom of the beaker

To make sure that all the acid has reacted.

Filter the mixture

To remove the unreacted copper oxide.

Heat the solution until about half of the water has evaporated.

If all the water is evaporated when the solution is heated, a white powder will form.

Leave the solution for the rest of the water to evaporate slowly

To make sure that crystals form.

Dry the crystals on tissue paper / other suitable method of drying.
sets.modelHtml: 16 The student should use sulfuric acid to make copper sulfate crystals, as hydrochloric acid will make copper chloride. Pour the acid into the beaker and warm it as the reaction is too slow at room temperature. Add the copper oxide a full spatula at a time and stir it until it dissolves to give a blue solution. Keep adding the copper oxide until there is some left on the bottom of the beaker. This will make sure that all the acid has reacted. Filter the mixture and the excess copper oxide will be on the filter paper. Collect the copper sulfate solution in an evaporating basin and heat the solution until about half of the water has evaporated. Leave the basin on a windowsill for the rest of the water to evaporate slowly and copper sulfate crystals will form. If all the water is evaporated when the solution is heated, the crystals will lose their water of crystallisation and turn to a white powder. Dry the crystals on tissue paper.
sets.partialHtml:
16 To make copper sulfate you need sulfuric acid because hydrochloric acid would make copper chloride.

Put the sulfuric acid in a beaker and add the copper oxide a spatula full at a time until there is some left in the bottom of the beaker. Stir it to help it to react. Filter the mixture. Collect the solution in an evaporating basin and heat it for a few minutes. Leave it to cool and the crystals will form. Filter the crystals and leave them to dry.

This candidate has included many of the important details for preparing pure, dry copper sulfate crystals, although they have omitted to warm the acid so the reaction would be very slow. They have also identified the correct acid to use, so this so this is a Level 2 answer and is awarded the higher mark. To achieve Level 3 the candidate should give more reasons for the improvements. For example, the copper oxide is added until there is some left in the bottom of the beaker to make sure that all the sulfuric acid has reacted.

4 out of 6 marks awarded.

17 A student carried out an experiment to investigate the temperature changes during the displacement reactions of copper sulfate solution.

They used the following outline procedure.

Measure 20 cm3 of copper sulfate solution and pour it into a polystyrene cup.

Record the temperature of the copper sulfate solution.

Weigh out 0.5 g of magnesium powder onto a watch glass.

Add the magnesium to the copper sulfate solution.

Record the highest temperature reached.

Repeat these four steps using iron and zinc powders instead of magnesium powder.

sets.modelHtml:
17.2 Order of reactivity is: magnesium, zinc, iron, copper.

The most reactive metal gives the highest temperature rise. The least reactive metal gives the lowest temperature rise. Copper is the least reactive, as all the other metals displace it from copper sulfate solution.

17.3 Measure 20 cm3 of copper sulfate solution using a measuring cylinder and pour it into a polystyrene cup. Put a thermometer into the solution and record the initial temperature. Use a balance to weigh 0.5 g of zinc powder onto a watch glass. Add the zinc powder to the copper sulfate solution and stir the mixture. Wait until the temperature stops rising and record the highest temperature reached. Repeat the experiment using 0.1 g, 0.2 g, 0.3 g and 0.4 g of zinc powder. The volume of copper sulfate must be the same in each experiment so that it is a fair test. I would expect the temperature rise to increase as the mass of zinc increases.
sets.partialHtml:
17.2 Magnesium is the most reactive metal as it gives the highest temperature rise, then zinc, then iron.

17.3 Use a measuring cylinder to measure the copper sulfate solution and place it in a polystyrene cup. Record the initial temperature with a thermometer.

Weigh 0.5 g of zinc powder on a watch glass then tip it into the copper sulfate solution. Record the final temperature.

Repeat the experiment using different masses of zinc.

As the mass of zinc increases the temperature increases.

17.2 The student has given the correct order for the three metals (magnesium, zinc and iron) and related the order to the temperature rise. However, they have not included copper in their list.

17.3 The student has included many of the essential practical details, so this is a Level 2 answer. The lower mark is awarded as there are a number of important omissions. The mixture should be stirred with the thermometer to enable the zinc to react with the copper sulfate solution, and the final temperature is the highest temperature reached. To move to Level 3, the student would need to suggest some possible masses of zinc to use. The student should also make sure that this is a fair test by keeping the volume of copper sulfate solution the same in each experiment so that the results are valid.

3 marks out of 6 awarded.

sets.questionHtml:
18 Draw and compare the reaction profiles of exothermic and endothermic reactions.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
18 Draw and compare the reaction profiles of exothermic and endothermic reactions.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref

18

Level 2: Scientifically relevant features are identified; the way(s) in which they are similar/different is made clear and (where appropriate) the magnitude of the similarity/difference is noted.

4–6

AO1.1

4.5.1.2 Chemistry 5.5.1.2 CS

Level 1: Relevant features are identified and differences noted.

1–3

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Axes drawn and labelled energy (y-axis) and progress of reaction (x-axis).

Horizontal lines drawn and labelled reactants and products.

Products line to the right of reactants.

Arrows drawn from reactants to products.

Labelled ΔH.

Curves drawn.

Activation energies labelled.

Exothermic reaction has products line at a lower energy than reactants line

But endothermic reaction has products line at a higher energy than reactants line.

ΔH arrow is pointing downwards for the exothermic reaction

Because energy is transferred to the surroundings / given out

But pointing upwards for the endothermic reaction

Because energy is taken in.

Both have activation energies from the reactants line to the top of the curve.

The activation energy for the endothermic reaction is greater than that for the exothermic reaction.

Credit can be given for all points on labelled diagrams.
sets.modelHtml:
18

The axes are the same for both diagrams. In an exothermic reaction, energy is given out so the energy change (ΔH) arrow points downwards, ΔH is negative and the products line is lower than the reactants line. In an endothermic reaction, energy is taken in so the ΔH arrow points upwards, ΔH is positive and products line is higher than the reactants line. In both diagrams the activation energy arrow starts at the reactants line and points up to the top of the curve. The activation energy is much larger for the endothermic reaction.
sets.partialHtml:
18

Both reactions have the same axes. The exothermic reaction has the products line lower than the reactants line but the endothermic reaction has the products line higher than the reactants line. The energy change for the exothermic reaction is negative as the arrow points downwards but the energy change of the endothermic reaction is positive as the arrow points upwards.

The student has drawn the diagrams with most of the labels correct and written some correct similarities and differences between them, so this answer is Level 2. Indicative content

Raw materials

Crude oil is finite or will run out or is non-renewable.

Crude oil needs to undergo fractional distillation to give ethene.

Ethene is only one of the fractions of crude oil.

Crude oil fractions may need to be cracked to produce sufficient quantities of ethene.

Sugar cane/beet is a renewable resource.

Sugar cane/beet requires land for growth.

Sugar cane/beet needs to be processed to release the glucose.

The processing of sugar cane/beet requires energy.

The remainder of the sugar cane/beet needs to be disposed of.

Conditions

Hydration requires more energy for higher temperature.

Hydration requires more energy to give higher pressure.

Hydration requires acid catalyst, which is more dangerous or corrosive or toxic than yeast.

Fermentation uses yeast, which some workers may be allergic to.

Equation

Hydration only produces a single product (so higher atom economy).

Hydration is a reversible reaction so (potentially) a lower yield.

Use of excess, cheap water or steam will shift equilibrium to the right to increase yield.

Fermentation produces gaseous by-product.

Fermentation releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere (which increases global warming).

Yeast catalyses an irreversible reaction so (potentially) a higher yield.
sets.modelHtml:
19 Sugar can be obtained from a plant called sugar beet, which is a renewable resource. However, ethene is obtained from crude oil, which is not renewable and is running out. In fact, the crude oil is processed, ethene is not the only compound obtained and so uses have to be found for these or they need to be broken down or cracked into ethene. Sugar beet is not perfect, though; it has to be processed itself by boiling, which requires energy and the ‘left overs’ of the sugar beet to be disposed of.

Hydration of ethene requires heating and a catalyst but the fermentation of sugar only uses yeast at about 30°C so is much more energy efficient.

The reaction between ethene and steam gives ethene so 100% atom economy, which is better than the fermentation method because waste carbon dioxide gas is made. This gas is also bad for the environment as it leads to global warming.

Overall, I would say that the fermentation method is better, but it is not without issues.
sets.partialHtml:

Using yeast will be much safer. There is more ethanol made in fermentation because there is two in front of the ethanol in the equation.

This student has made a simple judgement by stating that the fermentation method is better and by linking that with the fact that crude oil is running out. The student then just restates the conditions from the table without commenting on why these would be more expensive. Likewise, there is no explanation for why the use of yeast would be safer. The reference to the two moles of ethanol being formed in the fermentation equation does not mean that the yield is higher. This is a Level 2 response.

20 Plan a chromatography investigation to show that a green-coloured food dye contains two separate chemicals of different colours. The colours of these chemicals combine to give the green colour. One of the chemicals is more soluble in ethanol than the other.

You may include a sketch to illustrate your investigation and your plan should give
valid results.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
20 Plan a chromatography investigation to show that a green-coloured food dye contains two separate chemicals of different colours. The colours of these chemicals combine to give the green colour. One of the chemicals is more soluble in ethanol than the other.

You may include a sketch to illustrate your investigation and your plan should give
valid results.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref

20

Level 3: The method would lead to the production of a valid outcome. The key steps are identified and logically sequenced.

5–6

AO1

4.8.1.3

Level 2: The method would not necessarily lead to a valid outcome. Most steps are identified, but the method is not fully logically sequenced.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Method

Mark the start/origin line (in pencil) on chromatography paper.

Place (small) spots of green-coloured food dye on the line.

Add ethanol to the bottom of the beaker, which must be below the spots of dye.

Place the paper (gently) in the ethanol and the lid on the beaker (making sure the paper is secure).

Leave for the ethanol to travel up the paper.

Remove the paper from the beaker and (use a pencil to) mark the distance travelled by the ethanol or the solvent front.

Results

There will be two separate spots produced from the food dye.

One spot will be yellow, and the other spot will be blue.

[The above indicative content may be evidenced in an annotated sketch.]
sets.modelHtml:
20 My steps for the chromatography experiment are:

1. Carefully draw a pencil line 2 cm from the bottom of the paper.

2. Place two spots of the green food dye on the pencil line, making sure that they are not big.

3. Pour a 1 cm depth of ethanol into a beaker.

4. Wrap the top of the chromatography paper around a glass rod and gently place in the ethanol. The rod helps to stop the paper from collapsing into the ethanol. Place a lid on the top of the beaker.

5. Wait for the ethanol to move up the paper, and take it out when the ethanol is about
1 cm from the top. Use a pencil to mark how far the ethanol has moved.

A green colour is made from a mixture of yellow and blue. I decided that the yellow dye is more soluble than the blue one and so placed it higher up the paper.
sets.partialHtml:
20 I would do the following chromatography experiment.

Draw a pencil line about 3 cm from the bottom of the paper.

Put a couple of spots of the green food dye on the pencil line. Not too big.

Place about a 2 cm depth of ethanol in a beaker and gently place the chromatography paper in the ethanol. Put a lid on the top of the beaker.

Leave so that the ethanol moves up the paper.

The chromatography paper should be like my sketch. In my example the blue chemical is more soluble in the ethanol than the yellow one.

This student has written a plan which would be effective at separating the two chemicals in the food dye. The sequence of steps is clearly stated and given in a logical manner. There is no mention of removing the chromatography paper before it has reached the top and indicating how far the solvent has travelled (the solvent front). The sketch supports the description of the plan, and the expected results are clearly stated. However, it would have been helpful to have indicated how the two colours, blue and yellow, have been determined; namely that when combined together a green colour is seen.

5 out of 6 marks awarded.

21 Calcite is a mineral that contains calcium carbonate.

Arcanite is a mineral that contains potassium sulfate.

Samples of these two minerals have had their labels removed by mistake. These samples are currently labelled A and B.

Describe how samples of A and B could be chemically analysed in order to identify which sample is calcite and which sample is arcanite.

Your analysis should include valid results.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
21 Calcite is a mineral that contains calcium carbonate.

Arcanite is a mineral that contains potassium sulfate.

Samples of these two minerals have had their labels removed by mistake. These samples are currently labelled A and B.

Describe how samples of A and B could be chemically analysed in order to identify which sample is calcite and which sample is arcanite.

Your analysis should include valid results.

[6 marks]

Indicative content

Chemical analysis

Testing for positive metal ion

Add dilute hydrochloric acid to each sample.

Use a nichrome wire loop or spray metal solution or dip a wooden splint in solution.

Place the sample in a blue Bunsen flame.

Testing for negative ion

Crush samples of A and B and place in separate test tubes.

Add dilute hydrochloric acid to each sample.

Add barium chloride (solution) to the acidified sample of A and of B.

Results

Testing for metal ion

Calcium ions give an orange-red flame colour.

Potassium ions give a lilac flame colour.

Testing for negative ion

Fizzing after addition of dilute hydrochloric acid indicates the presence of carbonate ions.

The gas given off from the addition of hydrochloric acid could be bubbled through limewater; the formation of a cloudy solution indicates carbon dioxide gas given off.

The formation of a white precipitate after the addition of barium chloride indicates the presence of sulfate ions.

Identification

Calcite will give an orange-red flame colour or will fizz with acid.

Arcanite will give a lilac flame colour or will give a white precipitate/solid with barium chloride.

Only testing of the metal ion or of the negative ion is needed to identify the mineral.
sets.modelHtml:
21 First

Add hydrochloric acid to separate samples of A and B.

Result: One of the samples will fizz and the other won’t. The one that fizzes is the calcite, because carbonates break down and give off carbon dioxide. The other one must be arcanite.

Second

Divide the acid samples of A and B into two halves.

Third

Add barium chloride to each of the acid samples.

Result: One of the samples will produce a white precipitate and the other won’t. The one that goes white is arcanite because it is a sulfate. The other one must be calcite.

Fourth

Clean a nichrome wire by placing in a blue Bunsen flame.

Dip the cleaned wire into the acidified sample A and then place in the blue flame.
Observe the colour.

Repeat for the cleaning of the wire and then test sample B.

Result: The calcite sample will give an orange-red flame colour, whereas the arcanite will give a lilac colour.

In conclusion, calcite will give an orange-red flame colour and will fizz when acid is added. Arcanite will give a lilac flame colour and a white precipitate with barium chloride.

This mixture can be separated into different parts by fractional distillation using a fractionating column as shown in Figure 5.

22.1 Give the general formula of the alkane homologous series. [1 mark]

22.2 Compare the properties of hydrocarbon molecules in the bitumen fraction with those of the LPG fraction. Include reference to how this allows these molecules to be separated into fractions.

[6 marks]

22 Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons. Figure 5

This mixture can be separated into different parts by fractional distillation using a fractionating column as shown in Figure 5.

parts.html: 22.1 Give the general formula of the alkane homologous series. [1 mark]

22.2 Compare the properties of hydrocarbon molecules in the bitumen fraction with those of the LPG fraction. Include reference to how this allows these molecules to be separated into fractions.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO/

Spec. ref

22.1

CnH2n+2

1

AO1

4.7.1.1

22.2

Level 2: Scientifically relevant features are identified; the way(s) in which they are similar/different is made clear and (where appropriate) the magnitude of the similarity/difference is noted.

4–6

AO2

4.7.1.1

4.7.1.2

4.7.1.3

Level 1: Relevant features are identified and differences noted.

1–3

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Molecular properties

Similarity

Both are mixtures of hydrocarbons or reference to both not being one pure substance.

Differences

Reference to the different boiling points of the molecules /
LPG has a lower boiling point (than bitumen) / or reverse argument (ORA.)

Reference to the different viscosity of the molecules/
LPG are gases and flow easily but bitumen is a thick liquid and flows slowly.

Reference to the different flammability of the molecules/
LPG is very or highly flammable/burns easily but bitumen is not very flammable/does not burn easily.

Separation

Reference to the temperature gradient of the fractionating column.

Smaller molecules have lower boiling points / ORA.

Intermolecular forces between small molecules are weak(er) / ORA / Smaller molecules have less intermolecular forces / ORA.

The weaker the intermolecular forces then the less energy or heat is required to break them / ORA.

So LPG (at the top of the column) is made up of small(er) molecules

And bitumen (at the bottom of the column) is made up of large(r) molecules.
sets.modelHtml:
22.1 CnH2n+2

22.2 Compare means that I have to write about similarities and differences.

A similarity is that both the bitumen fraction and the LPG fraction are made up of mixture of hydrocarbons. In other words, they are not just one pure compound.

There are several differences – the G of LPG stands for ‘gases’ and the molecules in this fraction are all gases, which have low boiling points. By contrast, bitumen is a thick black liquid with a much higher boiling point. The gases are colourless, which is another difference. Also, the gases will move easily through the equipment as they are not very viscous, but the bitumen fraction is very viscous.

Separation – the different boiling points of the fractions allows them to be separated. LPG is at the top of the column because this fraction is made up of small molecules with weak forces between them. The bitumen fraction is at the bottom of the column where it is cooler. The molecules in bitumen are larger and have much stronger intermolecular forces, which results in a much higher boiling point. These stronger forces need a lot more heat to break.
sets.partialHtml:
22.1 CnH2n

22.2 The three properties of the hydrocarbons are boiling points, viscosity and flammability. The LPG fraction is made up of smaller molecules so it has a lower boiling point, flows easily and burns easily too. The bitumen fraction is the opposite because it is made up of larger molecules.

Separation of the fractions is due to the difference in their boiling points. As said the LPG fraction has a lower boiling point. This is because the molecules are smaller and so the forces between the molecules are weaker. This means that less energy is needed for boiling. The temperature at the top of the column is lower. So the LPG gases can rise to the top away from the heavier bitumen fraction.

markingExamples.answerHtml:
22.2 Compare means that I have to write about similarities and differences.

A similarity is that both the bitumen fraction and the LPG fraction are made up of mixture of hydrocarbons. In other words, they are not just one pure compound.

There are several differences – the G of LPG stands for ‘gases’ and the molecules in this fraction are all gases, which have low boiling points. By contrast, bitumen is a thick black liquid with a much higher boiling point. The gases are colourless, which is another difference. Also, the gases will move easily through the equipment as they are not very viscous, but the bitumen fraction is very viscous.

Separation – the different boiling points of the fractions allows them to be separated. LPG is at the top of the column because this fraction is made up of small molecules with weak forces between them. The bitumen fraction is at the bottom of the column where it is cooler. The molecules in bitumen are larger and have much stronger intermolecular forces, which results in a much higher boiling point. These stronger forces need a lot more heat to break.

Conical flask with bung and delivery tube to test tube of limewater

Clamp and stand

3 Measuring cylinders

Clock

Plan

Measure out 25 cm3 of sodium carbonate solution and add to the conical flask.

Measure out the ethanoic acid and add to the conical flask. Quickly put the bung in and start the clock.

Time how long it takes for the limewater to go cloudy.

Repeat steps 1 to 3 but instead of using ethanoic acid, use the same volume of hydrochloric acid that is of the same concentration.

26 Polymers A and B have a number of differences.

Properties

Polymer A is a thermoplastic polymer but polymer B is a thermosetting polymer.

The shape of polymer A can be changed by heat. However, the shape of polymer B is fixed and can’t be changed by heat because there are cross-links between the chains.

Types of polymerisation

Polymer A is made from an addition reaction whereas polymer B is made from a condensation reaction.

The reaction for polymer A only gives one product; however, the reaction for polymer B produces water as a by-product.

Types of monomer

Polymer A is made from an alkene monomer but polymer B is made from two monomers with one being a carboxylic acid at each end and the other monomer having an alcohol group at each end.

27 A catalyst is defined as something that speeds up the rate of a chemical reaction but is not changed by it. It does this by providing an alternative pathway for the reaction that has a lower activation energy.

The addition of manganese dioxide to the apparatus results in an increase in the volume of gas collected with time compared to the control. I think that this investigation does prove that manganese dioxide is a catalyst. It doesn’t investigate activation energy or reaction pathways but it does show that manganese dioxide does speed up the rate of the reaction and is not changed by it.

28 An example of an equilibrium system is that between dinitrogen tetraoxide and nitrogen dioxide. The equation is:

N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g)

colourless gas dark brown gas

The formation of nitrogen dioxide, NO2, is an endothermic reaction. At room temperature both gases are present in an equilibrium mixture.

Explain, by reference to Le Chatelier’s Principle, how the conditions of the equilibrium could be changed to increase the proportion of nitrogen dioxide in the equilibrium mixture.

[4 marks]

parts.html:

colourless gas dark brown gas

The formation of nitrogen dioxide, NO2, is an endothermic reaction. At room temperature both gases are present in an equilibrium mixture.

Explain, by reference to Le Chatelier’s Principle, how the conditions of the equilibrium could be changed to increase the proportion of nitrogen dioxide in the equilibrium mixture.

[4 marks]

(Because it is an endothermic reaction) the equilibrium will shift to the right.

sets.modelHtml:
28 Le Chatelier’s Principle states that if an equilibrium system experiences a change then it will adjust to counteract the effect of that change.

The equation has two moles on the right-hand side and only one on the left. This means that if the pressure is decreased then the equilibrium will shift to the side with more moles of gas or shift to give more nitrogen dioxide.

The reaction is endothermic and so if the temperature is increased then the equilibrium will shift to adsorb the extra heat or to the endothermic side, which also results in more nitrogen dioxide.

So increase the temperature but decrease the pressure.
sets.partialHtml:
28 The reaction mixture needs to be heated up and the pressure needs to go up too. The reaction is endothermic and so Le Chatelier’s Principle means that if the mixture is heated then the system will move to the right or to the endothermic side. This movement means that there is more nitrogen dioxide made. There will still be some dinitrogen tetraoxide in the mixture as the gases are still in equilibrium.

Both changes in the conditions are correctly stated, which are the lower level marking points at AO1. The response then explains that by increasing the temperature the equilibrium position will shift towards the products. This explanation is linked to the endothermic nature of the forward reaction and meets the first AO2 descriptor marking point. The reference to the presence of dinitrogen tetraoxide in the equilibrium mixture is correct but not required by the question and so does not gain credit. The response does not give any explanation for the increase in pressure and so the second AO2 descriptor marking point is not awarded.

3 out of 4 marks awarded.

sets.modelHtml:
29 I agree with the student saying that distilled water is pure, but I do not agree with fresh milk being a pure liquid. My reasoning is as follows.

I know that pure liquids have precise melting and boiling temperatures. The table shows that this is the case for distilled water but not for fresh milk. It is true that milk may be called pure in that it has not had anything added to it, but this is not what a chemist means by being pure.

The ‘follow-on’ milk is correctly identified as not being a pure liquid. Milk is a mixture of different things as it has calcium, protein and fat in it. The follow-on milk is a special formulation to help babies grow and has the right mixture of things for that.

The sea water is a bit odd because the table does show it having a specific boiling temperature, but I know that it is salt water or water with sodium chloride dissolved in it. So it isn’t a pure liquid but a mixture as stated by the student.
sets.partialHtml:

This means that the boiling temperature can change.

There is a clear judgement on the distilled water, which is logically linked to the data in the table. This means that it is above Level 1. However, the judgement on sea water is incorrect. It is expected that students know that sea water has salt in it and so is a mixture despite the specific data in the table. The comment on fresh milk does not actually give a judgement and leaves the reader unsure what the conclusion is about fresh milk. There is no comment made on the ‘follow-on’ milk. This is a Level 2 response.

30.1 The atmosphere is about 80% nitrogen and 20% oxygen and there is a small amount of carbon dioxide and water vapour.

30.2 I can see from the table that the carbon dioxide percentage has gone down by a huge amount. One reason for this is because green plants absorb carbon dioxide in photosynthesis. Another reason is because the carbon dioxide can dissolve in water or the oceans.

The photosynthesis by plants is also the reason for the change in the level of oxygen because plants are taking in carbon dioxide and giving out oxygen.

Nitrogen has increased because of volcanoes. These give off nitrogen when they erupt. They also give off water vapour, but this has condensed to form the oceans, which is why the amount of water vapour in the atmosphere is still only very low.

Lifestyle changes such as travel by bicycle instead of bus or train or car/taxi.

Use/install solar panels.

Use/install wind turbines or wave machines.

Use less energy or electricity by unplugging devices or turning lights off or use energy-saving bulbs or similar.

Reuse or recycle.

Accept any reasonable alternative answers.

(Decrease emissions of methane)

Any two from:

Reduce amount of beef or red meat eaten.

More organic farming.

Improve management of landfills.

Reduce fossil fuel extraction.

Accept any reasonable alternative answers.
sets.modelHtml:
31.1 The term ‘carbon footprint’ means the total amount of carbon dioxide that is given out during the lifetime of the product.

31.2 There are lots of ways to decrease the emissions of carbon dioxide as we can use cars less; for example, children could walk to school rather than being driven. Also, lots more houses and businesses could have solar panels so there is less demand for electricity from power stations fuelled by fossil fuels. Turning off lights when we leave rooms will also save electricity and so reduce CO2.

Two ways to reduce methane emissions are: (i) reduce the amount of cattle that produce methane by eating less red meat, possibly eating chicken/fish or even going veggie; (ii) landfill sites also produce methane so better management of these can help.

carbon monoxide.

[6 marks]

sets.modelHtml:
32 The five different gases given off during combustion are: CO2, CO, NO2, SO2 and soot.

Combustion can be complete if there is enough oxygen in the air or incomplete if there isn’t.

The equation for complete combustion is: C + O2 → CO2

The equation for incomplete combustion is: 2C + O2 → 2CO

Nitrogen gas is in the atmosphere and so when combustion occurs the heat from the reaction can make nitrogen and oxygen react. The equation is: N2 + 2O2 → 2NO2

The sulfur impurities in the fuel mean that sulfur can also react with oxygen.
The equation is: S + O2 → SO2

Soot can also be given off during incomplete combustion. It is made up of tiny particles of carbon, which are not good for people with asthma.

The sulfur dioxide is made from burning the sulfur impurities in the coal.

sets.modelHtml:
33.1 I would test for chlorine gas using a damp piece of blue litmus paper. If chlorine were present then the paper would be bleached.

33.2 I know that 20% of air is oxygen, so the test for this gas is to put a glowing splint in the gas. The positive result is for the splint to relight.

33.3 Sulfur dioxide gas can dissolve in rainwater to form acid rain. This rain can erode limestone buildings and can kill plants. It can also react with some metals such as in statues.

One other problem with sulfur dioxide is that if it is breathed in then it can cause breathing issues, especially for those with asthma.
sets.partialHtml:
33.1 Chlorine gas can be tested for with some blue litmus paper. The paper has to be made wet with water first and then put in the chlorine. The colour goes red first but then is bleached white.

33.2 Oxygen gas should be present in the atmosphere and it can be tested for with a glowing splint. A positive test will be a loud pop!

33.3 One of the problems of sulfur dioxide is that it will result in acid rain. This will then react with buildings made of limestone. You may not see it but there could be bubbles from the reaction. Acid rain can kill plants.

33.1 This is a correct answer and one which gives the extra detail of the paper going red before bleaching or white. Both marks awarded.

33.2 The test for oxygen gas is correct but the result has been confused with that for hydrogen gas. Only 1 mark awarded.

There is no mention of the respiratory problems and there are only two problems given that are associated with acid rain. Hence this is at the lower end of the level, which scores 3 marks.

6 out of 8 marks awarded.

sets.modelHtml:
34.1 There will be chemicals such as bleach in the wastewater that won’t be in the lake water.

34.2 The water from a lake would be treated by filtering it to remove solids such as twigs that might have fallen in and it would be sterilised by using chlorine to kill any bacteria that are in the water.

The water from the sea is salty water so this salt needs to be removed. This can be done at a desalination plant, where osmosis is used to separate the salt and the water. A membrane only allows the water through, which is then suitable to drink.
sets.partialHtml:
34.1 There will be bits of food and also soap bubbles in the water.

34.2 The water from a lake needs to be filtered first and then chlorine tablets can be added. These kill any bacteria that are in the water. They do make the water taste horrible but if it is left for a few hours then the chlorine goes and it’s much better to drink.

The sea water needs to have the salt removed. If the salt is not removed, then it can make a person go crazy. It used to happen a lot to sailors back in the day.

35 Plastic bottles are made from crude oil, which is a non-renewable resource; in other words it is running out. The recycling potential is quite low at 30% and 450 years is still quite a long time to stay in the environment before it breaks down. However, the amount of energy it takes to make them is very low.

Glass bottles are made from sand and limestone, which are easily found around us. The recycling potential is excellent at 100%. However, a lot of energy is needed to make them and they take a very, very long time to break down in the environment. Somehow I don’t seem to mind seeing a glass bottle on the ground as much as I do seeing a plastic bottle.

I prefer glass bottles to plastic ones. Yes, they take much longer to break down and more energy to make but once made they can be used over and over so there should be an energy benefit in the long run. It is true that glass can break much more easily than plastic and it is heavier so it takes more fuel for lorries to transport them about but I still think that the 100% recycling will mean that there is an energy benefit at the end.

sets.modelHtml:
36 The information in the table suggests that the higher the temperature then the less ammonia is made (e.g. only 11% at 50°C compared to 82% at 200°C at 100 atm) so a lower temperature is best. However, there is less of a decrease at the higher temperatures. The decrease is because the reaction to make ammonia is exothermic and Le Chatelier’s Principle states that an increase in temperature means that the reaction goes in the endothermic direction.

The information in the table also suggests that the higher the pressure then the more ammonia is made (e.g. only 11% at 100 atm compared to 42% at 500 atm for a temperature of 500°C).

So the best conditions for making ammonia are high pressure but a low temperature.

Industry is using a higher temperature, but this must be because the reaction rate is faster. A balance has to be made between rate and yield. It must be better to make less in a shorter period of time.

Industry could use a much higher pressure but doesn’t because to create a high pressure is costly due to the energy needed to achieve it and due to the expensive equipment that needs to be used.
sets.partialHtml:
36 The table shows that if the pressure is increased then more ammonia is made, and so industry should use high pressure. It may be that this is too expensive. The table also shows that if the temperature is decreased then more ammonia is made. This means that the best conditions are high pressure and low temperature. Industry should use a lower temperature because at 200 atm the percentage at 200°C is much higher at 89% compared to only 39% at 400°C. The figures for the temperature used by industry are not in the table, which is not helpful.

There is a clear judgement made on the best conditions for the production of ammonia and this is logically linked to the data in the table. This means that it is above Level 1. However, the judgement is not linked to the chemical reasons for these conditions. This means that this response is at Level 2. There is a brief reference to the cost of higher pressure, but this is not sufficient for the top end of Level 2. Students are expected to estimate or predict the percentages for the conditions used by industry that are not in the table.

3 out of 6 marks awarded.

sets.modelHtml: 01.2 Put the slide in the centre of the stage and use the clips to hold it. Move the lowest power objective lens over the slide and look through the eyepiece lens. You may need to adjust the lamp or mirror to make sure the view is bright enough. Not looking through the eyepiece, use the coarse focusing dial to move the lens down until it is almost touching the slide. Now looking through the eyepiece, use the coarse focusing dial to move the lens upwards until the image becomes clear. Now use the fine focusing dial to get a really sharp image. 03 The first transplant of a synthetic organ took place in 2011.

Doctors used an artificial trachea (windpipe) made from plastic coated with stem cells from the patient’s own bone marrow.

The alternative would have been to wait for a suitable trachea from a human donor.

Evaluate the benefits of transplanting an artificial trachea coated with a patient’s own stem cells compared with transplanting a trachea from another person.

[6 marks]

Evaluate the benefits of transplanting an artificial trachea coated with a patient’s own stem cells compared with transplanting a trachea from another person.

[6 marks]

Benefits of using an artificial trachea
