sets.modelHtml: 03 If you transplant a trachea from another person then you might have to wait a long time until a suitable donor becomes available. Also, unless the donor is a very close relative there is a high chance of the transplant being rejected. However, if you use an artificial trachea covered in the patient’s own cells then the transplant can happen much sooner as you don’t need to wait for a donor and it probably won’t be rejected. You can also make it exactly the right size to suit the patient. So an artificial transplant is probably the best option, although as it is a relatively new technique there may be some side effects we don’t know about yet.
sets.partialHtml:
03 The artificial trachea has been covered in the patient’s own stem cells, which will not be rejected because the patient’s immune system will recognise that the cells are the patient’s own. If a real trachea from another donor was used then it could be rejected, or else the patient would have to be given drugs to knock out their immune system to prevent rejection. This could leave the patient vulnerable to other infections. Also, a real trachea can only be used if a donor dies (or possibly if they had their own lung transplant and their trachea could be used for this patient). This means that there is usually a long waiting list for a trachea that is not damaged by age, accident or illness and is the right size too. In conclusion, I believe the advantages of using the artificial trachea outweigh any disadvantages.

The points made in this answer are explained well and relevant additional points to those on the mark scheme are made too. Level 2 can be awarded as a judgement is also made. However, when a question asks for an evaluation you should always look to see if you can make points to support both sides of an argument before you make your final judgement. If the student had attempted that here, they could have gained a Level 3.

4 out of 6 marks awarded.

The potato in B gained mass because it absorbed water by osmosis, which is when water moves from a dilute solution (salt solution) to a more concentrated solution (potato) through a partially permeable membrane. The potato in A was also in a more dilute solution (than the potato) but it wasn’t as dilute as B, so the potato only went up to 5.4 g not
5.8 g. The potatoes in C and D both lost water because they were in more concentrated solutions. D was the most concentrated, so the potato lost more water.

05 Compare the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
05 Compare the processes of diffusion, osmosis and active transport.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO /

Spec. ref.

05

Level 2: Scientifically relevant features are identified; the way(s) in which they are similar/different is made clear and (where appropriate) the magnitude of the similarity/difference is noted.

4–6

AO1

4.1.3.1

4.1.3.2

4.1.3.3

Level 1: Relevant features are identified and differences noted.

1–3

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Similarities

Diffusion, osmosis and active transport are processes that move substances in and out of cells.

In osmosis and diffusion, particles move from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.

Osmosis is a particular example of diffusion.

Osmosis and diffusion do not require energy / are passive processes.

Osmosis and active transport (and sometimes diffusion) involve cell membranes.

Differences

Any substance (in solution or gas) can diffuse, whereas osmosis is the diffusion of water only.

Osmosis only occurs across a partially permeable membrane; diffusion can occur across a membrane or without a membrane; active transport only occurs across membranes.

Active transport requires energy (from respiration); osmosis and diffusion do not require energy / are passive processes.

Active transport can move substances from an area of lower concentration to an area of higher concentration / against a concentration gradient; osmosis and diffusion only move substances from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration / down a concentration gradient.
sets.modelHtml: 05 Diffusion, osmosis and active transport are all ways that substances can move in and out of cells. Diffusion is movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration. Osmosis is a type of diffusion but it only applies to the movement of water across a partially permeable membrane. Active transport is different because substances move from a low concentration to a higher concentration – which is the opposite of diffusion (and osmosis). Active transport needs energy to move things up the concentration gradient. Diffusion and osmosis do not need energy because they move things down a concentration gradient.
sets.partialHtml:

Osmosis is the net movement of water from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane. Active transport uses energy to move particles against a concentration gradient from an area of lower concentration to an area of higher concentration.

The student has given full, correct definitions of the three processes but has not followed the command word ‘compare’, which requires the student to explicitly describe the similarities and/or differences between them. Therefore, this answer is limited to Level 1.

sets.modelHtml: 08 Heart valves make sure that blood flows in the correct direction through the heart, so the right side pumps blood to the lungs to collect oxygen and the left side then pumps the blood all around the body. This ensures that oxygen gets to all body cells. If the heart valves are faulty, blood doesn’t flow as efficiently and might not all go in the right direction. This might mean that oxygen doesn’t get quickly enough to the places that need it, like our muscles if we are exercising. Oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration to give us energy, so without enough oxygen you will get less energy and so will be tired and out of breath. Your muscles might have to do anaerobic respiration, but this doesn’t give us as much energy and the lactic acid can also make you tired.
sets.partialHtml:
08 If a heart valve doesn’t work properly then not all the blood flows in the right direction. This means that not all the blood that’s meant to go to the lungs does go there. This means that not all the oxygen is collected from the lungs so you get out of breath and get very tired. This is particularly bad if you try to exercise, when you need more oxygen to give you the extra energy you need.

The points made in this answer are explained clearly and in a logical sequence. This is a good Level 2 answer. However, one key idea that is missing is the reason why oxygen is needed to give you energy. If the student had also explained that most of our energy comes from aerobic respiration, or that with less oxygen getting to the muscles there will be less aerobic respiration, then Level 3 could have been awarded.

4 out of 6 marks awarded.

sets.questionHtml:
10 Compare the structure and function of xylem and phloem tissues.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
10 Compare the structure and function of xylem and phloem tissues.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO /

Spec. ref.

10

Level 2: Scientifically relevant features are identified; the way(s) in which they are similar/different is made clear and (where appropriate) the magnitude of the similarity/difference is noted.

4–6

AO1

4.2.3.2

Level 1: Relevant features are identified and differences noted.

1–3

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Similarities

Xylem and phloem are both plant transport tissues.

Differences

Xylem is made of hollow/dead tubes; phloem is made of tubes of (elongated/living) cells.

Xylem walls are strengthened by lignin; phloem walls are not strengthened by lignin.

Phloem cells have pores in their end walls (to allow sap to move); xylem does not have pores.

Xylem transports water and mineral ions; phloem transports (dissolved) sugars.

Xylem transports (water and mineral ions) from the roots to the stems and leaves; phloem transports (dissolved sugars) from the leaves to the rest of the plant.

Xylem is the site of transpiration; phloem is the site of translocation.
sets.modelHtml: 10 Xylem and phloem are both tubes that carry substances through a plant. Xylem is made of dead hollow cells that carry water and mineral ions from the soil up the stem to the leaves, where the water evaporates into the air. This is called transpiration. Phloem is made of living cells which carry dissolved sugars both up and down the plant. It moves sugar from places like leaves where it’s made, to places like fruit or roots where it’s stored or to places like new shoots or buds where it’s needed for growth. This is called translocation. Xylem cells have lignin to give them strength, but phloem cells are full of sap to give them support. Phloem cells have holes (pores) so sap can move from one cell to the next.
sets.partialHtml:
10 Transpiration occurs through the xylem. This is where water and dissolved mineral ions are carried from the roots up through the stem to the leaves, where the water then evaporates. The phloem is where translocation happens. This is when sugar made in the leaves by photosynthesis travels to other parts of the plant like growing roots and shoots and fruit. The sugar can be moved up or down the plant but water and mineral ions only move up the plant.

Indicative content

Points in favour of the effectiveness of vaccinating

As the percentage of people vaccinated increases, the number of cases decreases.

The pattern is consistent over 38/many years.

The greatest increase in the percentage vaccinated (1980–1990) corresponds (approximately) with the greatest fall in number of cases.

As the percentage vaccinated has stayed high/above 70%, the number of cases has stayed (relatively) low/continued to decrease.

The dip in percentage vaccinated 1998–2003 corresponds with a (slight) rise in the number of cases.

The data involves very large number/millions of people over many/38 years.

Points against the effectiveness of vaccinating

Although there is a correlation between the increase in the percentage vaccinated and the fall in the number of cases, this does not prove that the vaccinations were responsible (although it seems likely).
sets.modelHtml: 12 The percentage of people immunised goes up quite steeply for the first 10 years and then continues to go up, apart from a few dips, for the next nearly 30 years. Over the same time, overall the number of cases falls fairly steeply for the first 15 years and then more slowly for the rest of the graph. So although one graph isn’t the exact mirror image of the other, there does seem to be a strong link and vaccinating people against measles does seem to have a real effect. The fact that this pattern involves millions of people over nearly 40 years shows it’s not a fluke.

13 Monoclonal antibodies can be used to treat cancer by delivering treatment substances directly to cancer cells without harming other body cells.

The treatment substances may be radioactive or toxic to kill the cancer cells, or they may be drugs that stop cancer cells growing and dividing.

Describe how monoclonal antibodies can be made so they will deliver the treatment substances directly to a patient’s cancer cells.

[6 marks]

Indicative content

Monoclonal antibodies are produced from a single clone of cells.

The antibodies are specific to a binding site/protein/antigen on the patient’s cancer cells.

Mouse lymphocytes are stimulated to make the
correct antibody.

The (mouse) lymphocytes are combined with a (particular type of) tumour cell

To make a hybridoma cell.

The hybridoma cell can (both) divide and make
the antibody.

Single hybridoma cells are cloned to produce many identical cells.

sets.modelHtml: 13 Take some of the patient’s cancer cells and get mouse lymphocyte cells (white blood cells) to make antibodies against the antigens on the cancer cells. Then join the mouse lymphocyte cells with a tumour cell (not the patient’s cancer cells) to make a new type of cell, which is a hybridoma. The hybridoma divides to make lots of identical cells (clones) that all make the same type of antibodies (monoclonal antibodies). Then you join the antibodies to a radioactive substance or a toxin that will kill the cancer cells. Because the antibodies only attach to the patient’s cancer cells then only the cancer cells are killed and other healthy cells are not damaged.
sets.partialHtml:
13 First you get a mouse lymphocyte cell that makes antibodies that will attach to the patient’s cancer cells. You combine that lymphocyte with a tumour cell to make a new cell called a hybridoma. That hybridoma then makes lots of antibodies that are all the same, which is why they are called monoclonal antibodies. You attach the drug that will kill the cancer cells to the monoclonal antibodies, so they can carry the drug straight to the patient’s cancer cells and not harm the surrounding cells, which is what cancer drugs normally do (which is why you usually get ill from cancer treatments).

This is a good answer and would gain Level 2 because of the amount of correct, relevant detail. However, there is one important detail missing, which is that the hybridoma cell is cloned (divides) to make lots of identical cells all making the same (monoclonal) antibody. Adding in this detail would have gained full marks.

5 out of 6 marks awarded.

14 Plants have different types of defence responses to resist microorganisms or herbivores:

physical

chemical

mechanical.

Describe examples of the three types of plant defence responses.

In your answer include which types of organism each type of defence response is most effective against.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
14 Plants have different types of defence responses to resist microorganisms or herbivores:

physical

chemical

mechanical.

Describe examples of the three types of plant defence responses.

In your answer include which types of organism each type of defence response is most effective against.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO /

Spec. ref.

14

Level 2: Scientifically relevant facts, events or processes are identified and given in detail to form an accurate account.

4–6

AO1

4.3.3.2

Level 1: Facts, events or processes are identified and simply stated but their relevance is not clear.

1–3

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Physical defence responses

To resist invasion of microorganisms

e.g. cellulose cell walls

e.g. tough waxy cuticle on leaves

e.g. layers of dead cells around stems (bark on trees), which fall off.

Chemical defence responses

To resist invasion of microorganisms

e.g. antibacterial chemicals.

To resist herbivores

e.g. poisons.

Mechanical defence responses

To resist herbivores

e.g. thorns/hairs

e.g. leaves that droop/curl when touched

e.g. mimicry to trick animals.
sets.modelHtml: 14 Examples of physical defences are tough cell walls made of cellulose and tough leaf cuticles made of wax. These stop microorganisms from getting into the plant. Examples of chemical defences are antibacterial chemicals to kill bacteria or poisons that stop animals eating the plant. Mechanical defences are things such as thorns that put off animals or hairs that make it difficult for insects to get to the leaves to eat them.
sets.partialHtml:
14 Different plants have different defences. Cactus plants have spines to stop animals eating them. They also have a tough waxy outer layer. This is partly to stop them drying out but it also makes it difficult for animals to chew through. This applies to big animals like camels as well as small insects. These are physical defences. Other plants have chemical defences and are poisonous to animals that try to eat them. For example, some berries are poisonous. Mechanical adaptations are like the mimosa plant where the leaves droop or curl if they are touched which makes it harder for animals to eat them. Plants can also be attacked by microorganisms which can get in if there is an opening. This is why if you cut the bark of a tree it will grow back to protect the tree from microorganisms (like cut skin on a human grows back).

There are some shortcomings in the answer, for example, cactus spines are usually classed as a mechanical defence. However, examples have been given of each type of defence as well as what they are protecting the plant against. There is enough detail to gain Level 2. Further examples could have been given, however; for instance, that chemical defences can also defend against bacteria.

5 out of 6 marks awarded.

Method

Place one of the coloured bulbs a set distance from
the pondweed.

Turn the bulb on and allow time for (the rate of photosynthesis of) the pondweed to adjust.

Count the number of bubbles of oxygen in a set time.

Repeat several times to get a mean/average count.

Control variables

Brightness/intensity/power of bulb

Temperature of water

sets.modelHtml: 15 Use the ruler to measure the distance between the beaker with the pondweed in and the red lamp. Keep this distance the same throughout the experiment. Turn the lamp on (make sure the lamp does not get wet) and leave it for a few minutes for the pondweed to get used to the light and start to give off oxygen bubbles. Count the number of bubbles given off by the pondweed in 5 minutes. Then repeat this but with the green lamp at the same distance. Repeat the whole thing two more times until you have three results for red light and three for green light. Make sure everything else stays the same, including the pondweed and the temperature of the water. If the hypothesis is correct, then the number of bubbles with the red light will always be greater than the number of bubbles with the green light.
sets.partialHtml:
15 You first put the red lamp a certain distance, say 30 cm, from the pondweed and turn it on. Count the number of bubbles in 1 minute. Repeat this three times and take an average. Then put the green lamp the same distance from the pondweed and repeat the counting as before. This is important to make sure both bulbs are the same brightness. If the average number of bubbles is higher with the red lamp than with the green lamp, then the hypothesis is correct.

This answer gains Level 3. Although some detail has been omitted, such as the need to keep the water temperature constant, the key steps have been described in a logical sequence and this method would lead to a valid outcome.

sets.questionHtml:
16 Compare the processes of aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
16 Compare the processes of aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO /

Spec. ref.

16

Level 2: Scientifically relevant features are identified; the way(s) in which they are similar/different is made clear and (where appropriate) the magnitude of the similarity/difference is noted.

4–6

AO1

4.4.2.1

4.4.2.2

Level 1: Relevant features are identified and differences noted.

1–3

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Similarities

Glucose is broken down

To transfer/release energy

Endothermic reaction

Occurs in living cells

Differences

Aerobic respiration uses oxygen; anaerobic respiration does not.

Aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid.

Equation for aerobic respiration is:

glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; equation for anaerobic respiration is: glucose → lactic acid

Aerobic respiration transfers/releases more energy (from the same amount of glucose) than anaerobic respiration.

Aerobic respiration is complete oxidation of glucose; anaerobic respiration is incomplete oxidation of glucose.

Aerobic respiration occurs in all living cells; anaerobic respiration occurs (mainly) in muscle cells.

Aerobic respiration occurs all the time (if there is enough oxygen present); anaerobic respiration occurs when there is not enough oxygen.

Lactic acid (build-up) from anaerobic respiration can cause oxygen debt and muscle fatigue; this does not happen in aerobic respiration.
sets.modelHtml: 16 Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to release energy from glucose, producing carbon dioxide and water. This takes place in every cell in the body. Anaerobic respiration also releases energy from glucose, but not as much as aerobic respiration because it doesn’t use oxygen, so the glucose is not completely oxidised. This takes place in muscles if they can’t get enough oxygen, for example during exercise. There are different types of anaerobic respiration but in humans lactic acid is the only product. This can build up in muscles and cause them to ache. This is called oxygen debt, because later on oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid.
sets.partialHtml:
16 Respiration is releasing energy from glucose. If oxygen is used for this it is called aerobic respiration. If oxygen is not used it is called anaerobic respiration. If you are exercising and can’t breathe in oxygen quickly enough then your muscles use anaerobic respiration so they can keep working. Aerobic respiration produces carbon dioxide and water but anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid.

Aerobic respiration is: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy

Anaerobic respiration is: glucose → lactic acid + some energy

The student has described both similarities and differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration. By saying that while both processes release energy, aerobic releases more, they have also described ‘the magnitude of the similarity/difference’. By fully matching the level descriptor this answer clearly gains Level 2. While it is not necessary to include all the indicative content to gain full marks, in this case there are, however, several additional points on the mark scheme that could also be made.

5 out of 6 marks awarded.

Similarities

Blood glucose (concentration) is not controlled / can go too high.

Differences

In Type 1, the pancreas does not make (sufficient) insulin; in Type 2, the pancreas still makes
(enough) insulin.

In Type 2, body cells no longer respond to insulin; in Type 1, body cells do respond to insulin.

Type 1 is (normally) treated with insulin injections;
Type 2 is not treated with insulin injections.

Type 2 can be treated by a carbohydrate-controlled diet and exercise regime; Type 1 can only be partly treated by a carbohydrate-controlled diet and exercise regime.

Obesity is a risk factor for Type 2 but not Type 1.
sets.modelHtml: 20.2 Type 1 diabetes is when your pancreas doesn’t make any or enough insulin. This means that excess glucose isn’t stored as glycogen, and blood glucose levels can go too high. However, you can treat it by injecting insulin. Type 2 diabetes can also cause your blood glucose to go too high but the problem is not your pancreas. The problem is that the body doesn’t respond properly to insulin, so injecting more makes no difference. Instead you control your blood glucose levels by diet and exercise. You don’t eat a lot of sugary or carbohydrate food at one time, or if you do, you exercise to use it up. Also controlling your diet and exercising is good to keep your weight down, which can help prevent Type 2 diabetes in the first place.
sets.partialHtml:
20.2 Both types of diabetes mean that you have problems controlling the level of glucose sugar in the blood. If it goes either too high or too low, it can cause serious health issues. Type 2 diabetes can happen if you are overweight and it has to be treated by controlling how much sugar or other carbohydrates you eat. How much you eat also depends on how much physical activity you do. If you have Type 1 diabetes you need regular insulin injections because your body is not making enough.

The student has described both a similarity and differences between the two types of diabetes. Everything in their answer is correct, but it is lacking in detail. So, although it gains Level 2 it does not gain full marks.

3 out of 4 marks awarded.

The problem is that the body doesn’t respond properly to insulin, so injecting more makes no difference. Instead you control your blood glucose levels by diet and exercise. You don’t eat a lot of sugary or carbohydrate food at one time, or if you do, you exercise to use it up. Also controlling your diet and exercising is good to keep your weight down, which can help prevent Type 2 diabetes in the first place.

sets.questionHtml:
22 Explain, using an example, why negative feedback is a necessary part of homeostasis.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
22 Explain, using an example, why negative feedback is a necessary part of homeostasis.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO /

Spec. ref.

22

Level 3: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, given in detail and logically linked to form a clear account.

5–6

AO1

4.5.1

4.5.3.2

4.5.3.7

Level 2: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, and there are attempts at logically linking. The resulting account is not fully clear.

3–4

Level 1: Points are identified and stated simply, but their relevance is not clear and there is no attempt at logical linking.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Homeostasis is the regulation of the internal conditions of a cell/organism to maintain optimum conditions for function (in response to internal/external changes).

Homeostasis maintains optimal conditions for enzyme action/cell functions.

Negative feedback is the process in which a change in a condition from a set level causes further actions that return the condition to its set level

e.g. regulation of blood glucose concentration: if blood glucose concentration is too high, the pancreas produces insulin that causes excess glucose to move from the blood into cells / be stored as glycogen in liver and muscle cells.

If blood glucose concentration is too low, the pancreas releases glucagon that causes stored glycogen to be converted into glucose and move into the blood.

Other examples include: regulation of body temperature; regulation of water levels; control of thyroxine levels.
sets.modelHtml: 22 Homeostasis means maintaining constant conditions inside the body. So if your blood glucose goes too high you need to bring it down, or if it falls too low you need to bring it back up. This happens automatically by negative feedback, which is when a change in one direction is corrected by the body making a change in the opposite direction to bring things back to normal. So if blood glucose goes too high, the pancreas releases insulin, which turns excess glucose into glycogen, which is stored in liver and muscle cells, bringing the blood glucose level back to normal. If the blood glucose level falls below normal then the pancreas releases glucagon, which turns glycogen back into glucose until the level of glucose in the blood is back up to normal.
sets.partialHtml:
22 Negative feedback is when a change causes the body to respond in a way that reverses the original change. For example, if you get too hot your body responds to cool you down, or if you are too cold your body responds to warm you up. It’s called negative feedback because it causes the opposite of the original change. The other kind of feedback is called positive feedback, but this makes things worse. For example, if you were too hot, positive feedback would make you even hotter. Homeostasis is about keeping conditions inside the body the same so we need negative feedback to do this, not positive feedback.

This answer would gain Level 2. All the points made are relevant and linked together logically. However, to gain Level 3 there needs to be more detail. For example, if the chosen example were regulation of blood glucose concentration, the roles of the different hormones involved would need to be clearly described.

4 out of 6 marks awarded.

23 A student wants to investigate how light affects the growth of newly germinated seedlings.

They are going to use the apparatus in Figure 10.

Figure 10

The student made the hypothesis:

‘Cress seedlings grow towards light.’

Plan an investigation to test this hypothesis.

You can use the apparatus in Figure 10 or any other apparatus you might need.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
23 A student wants to investigate how light affects the growth of newly germinated seedlings.

They are going to use the apparatus in Figure 10.

Figure 10

The student made the hypothesis:

‘Cress seedlings grow towards light.’

Plan an investigation to test this hypothesis.

You can use the apparatus in Figure 10 or any other apparatus you might need.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO /

Spec. ref.

23

Level 3: The method would lead to the production of a valid outcome. The key steps are identified and logically sequenced.

5–6

AO2

4.5.4.1

Level 2: The method would not necessarily lead to a valid outcome. Most steps are identified, but the method is not fully logically sequenced.

3–4

Level 1: The method plan would not lead to a valid outcome. Some relevant steps are identified, but links are not made clear.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Method

Place one dish of seedlings in conditions where light comes from one side only, e.g. inside a box with a hole in one side.

Place an identical dish of seedlings in conditions either where light comes from all around or where they are in the dark, e.g. inside box with no openings.

Make sure dishes are kept watered/moist.

Leave dishes for several days until seedlings have noticeably grown.

Compare the direction of growth of the seedlings in the
two dishes.

Control variables

Number/type of seedlings

Identical dish and cotton wool

Temperature

Amount of water

Time

Other variables

Independent variable is direction light is coming from.

Dependent variable is direction of growth.

Additional apparatus

Depends on details of investigation, e.g. scissors, lamp(s).

Safety

Avoid contact between any electrical equipment and water.
sets.modelHtml: 23 Grow 20 cress seedlings on moist cotton wool in a Petri dish. Cover half of the seedlings with a lightproof cover, e.g. tin foil or black paper. Make sure that it doesn’t squash the seedlings, though, and that they still have room to grow. Then put the dish somewhere where the light is coming from one side, such as on a windowsill in a room where the main lights are switched off. Leave it for a few days, making sure that it gets enough water. After a few days, remove the lightproof cover. If the hypothesis is true, then the seedlings in the dark will have grown straight up and the uncovered seedlings will grow towards the light. It is a fair test because all the seedlings have had the same conditions of temperature and water and been left for the same amount of time. It has been repeated because you’ve used quite a few seedlings, but to make sure you can do the whole experiment again.
sets.partialHtml:
23 You get two dishes of cress seedlings that are identical to begin with. Put one dish in a lightproof box and leave it for 3 days. Put the other one in a box that has a large hole cut in one side so that light comes from one side. Make sure you keep them both watered. After 3 days the seedlings in the lightproof box will have grown straight up but those in the other box will have grown towards the side where the light is coming in, proving the hypothesis.

This answer gains Level 3. Some details have been missed out, for example about controlling some of the variables, but there is enough information for another student to follow this plan and obtain valid results.

5 out of 6 marks awarded.

sets.title: Sexual and asexual reproduction
sets.sourceHeading: Question (SD; Explain; Biology only)	Sexual and asexual reproduction
sets.questionHtml:
24 Figure 11 shows insects called aphids feeding on a plant.

Figure 11

Winged aphids are able to fly and find a suitable food plant. They then reproduce asexually on the food plant for several generations. These offspring do not have wings.

Later, when the food plant becomes very crowded with aphids, or if there is not much food left, the aphids reproduce sexually. These offspring do have wings.

Explain the advantages for aphids of being able to reproduce both asexually and sexually.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
24 Figure 11 shows insects called aphids feeding on a plant.

Figure 11

Winged aphids are able to fly and find a suitable food plant. They then reproduce asexually on the food plant for several generations. These offspring do not have wings.

Later, when the food plant becomes very crowded with aphids, or if there is not much food left, the aphids reproduce sexually. These offspring do have wings.

Explain the advantages for aphids of being able to reproduce both asexually and sexually.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO /

Spec. ref.

24

Level 3: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, given in detail and logically linked to form a clear account.

5–6

AO2

4.6.1.1

4.6.1.3

Level 2: Relevant points (reasons/causes) are identified, and there are attempts at logically linking. The resulting account is not fully clear.

3–4

Level 1: Points are identified and stated simply, but their relevance is not clear and there is no attempt at logical linking.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Advantages of reproducing asexually

Can reproduce quickly

Producing many offspring to exploit food plant.

(Reproduce quickly as) they do not need to find a mate / only need one parent.

If food plant is suitable for parent then it will also be suitable for the offspring

As they are genetically identical/clones.

Offspring being wingless saves energy/resources.

Wings not needed as already on a suitable food plant.

Advantages of reproducing sexually

Offspring are winged so can disperse/fly away

To find (new/favourable) food plants.

Variation in offspring

Increases chance of at least some offspring finding (favourable) food plants (in dispersal stage) / gives
survival advantage.
sets.modelHtml: 24 Asexual reproduction produces genetically identical offspring (unlike sexual reproduction). It is also quicker than finding a mate. This means that when an aphid finds a plant that suits it, it reproduces asexually, producing lots of other aphids that will also be suited to the plant. They also don’t have wings because they don’t need them, and it would be a waste having them. However, when the plant becomes crowded and there is not enough food, the aphids need to have wings to fly away to find new food plants. This time they reproduce sexually because they don’t know what plants or conditions the offspring are going to find, so it’s best to have variation among them so at least some of them will be suited to the new conditions. It increases the survival chances of the offspring.
sets.partialHtml:
24 When an aphid finds a new plant and starts reproducing, reproducing asexually is quicker and more efficient as they do not have to find mates. The offspring will all be identical clones, so if the parent aphid is well adapted to the plant then so will all the offspring too. When the plant becomes very crowded, reproducing sexually to produce offspring with wings means that they can then fly off to find new plants to feed on.

The first part of the answer, about asexual reproduction, is explained well and is of Level 3 standard. However, more detail could have been given to the second part of the answer, explaining that sexual reproduction produces variation in the offspring and the benefits of this. Overall, therefore, this answer gains Level 2.

4 out of 6 marks awarded.

25 Describe how the structure of DNA is related to its functions.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
25 Describe how the structure of DNA is related to its functions.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO /

Spec. ref.

25

Level 2: Scientifically relevant facts, events or processes are identified and given in detail to form an accurate account.

4–6

AO1

4.6.1.2

4.6.1.4

4.6.1.5

4.6.2.1

4.6.2.2

4.8

Level 1: Facts, events or processes are identified and simply stated but their relevance is not clear.

1–3

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

DNA is a double strand/double helix.

DNA/double helix coils to form chromosomes.

DNA/double helix replicates/doubles

To form two copies of each chromosome

In the process of cell division/mitosis/meiosis/ during
cell cycle.

(This is) necessary for growth/development/reproduction.

Each strand is a sequence of four nucleotides/bases/
A, T, C, G.

The two strands have complementary base sequences.

A pairs with T; C pairs with G.

Base sequence carries genetic information/genes.

Base sequence codes for amino acid sequence

(And so) codes for a particular protein.

Base sequence determines the order that amino acids brought by carrier molecules to a ribosome are added to the growing protein chain

During protein synthesis.

The amino acid sequence of a protein determines its shape/job.

Each amino acid is coded for by a sequence of three bases.

A change in DNA structure/base sequence is a mutation.

A mutation can sometimes lead to a change in the amino acid sequence and a change in the final protein.

The protein may have a different shape and properties.

Many mutations lead to no/small change in protein so its appearance/function is not changed.

Some mutations lead to a major change in structure/shape/activity of protein, e.g. the active site of an enzyme may no longer fit the substrate or a structural protein may lose strength.

Not all DNA codes for proteins.

Some non-coding DNA can switch other genes on/off /affect gene expression.

Some mutations will lead to new phenotypes/variation in
a population.

(If the new phenotype is suited to an environmental change) this can lead to a change in the species/evolution

Through natural selection

Which may result in the formation of a new species/speciation.
sets.modelHtml:
25 The function of DNA is to carry genetic information in the form of a code, which is then used to make proteins (protein synthesis). When cells divide by mitosis or meiosis the DNA has to replicate, so that is another function. It carries the code in the form of a sequence of bases
(A, T, C and G). Reading along a DNA strand, every three bases codes for an amino acid, so a length of DNA codes for the amino acids that go to make up a protein. DNA is made of two complementary strands twisted into a helix shape. Complementary means that A on one strand pairs with T on the other, and C on one strand pairs with G on the other. Before a cell can divide, DNA makes an identical copy of itself. This is called DNA replication and it means that each new cell has copies of every gene and chromosome. Sometimes a mistake is made in the copying and perhaps just one base is different. This is called a mutation. Some mutations have no effect, but some can change the protein that is made. This can cause variation and is how natural selection and evolution happen.
sets.partialHtml:
25 DNA has a double helix structure. Each strand is made of a sequence of four bases,
T, A, G and C. The bases are like the letters of the genetic code and the order of the bases spells out the code of each gene. Genes work by telling cells to make proteins and the order of bases in the DNA codes for the order of the amino acids in each protein. Proteins are important because they are what our cells are made from, and some proteins are enzymes that control the chemical processes in our cells and body.

The student has both described the structure of DNA as well as explaining how this helps in its role in protein synthesis, and so has achieved Level 2 for linking the two ideas together. However, they have not mentioned other details, for example about how DNA structure can lead to mutations which are necessary for evolution, which would have allowed more marks to be awarded.

4 out of 6 marks awarded.

28 Compare the processes of selective breeding and genetic engineering.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
28 Compare the processes of selective breeding and genetic engineering.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO /

Spec. ref.

28

Level 2: Scientifically relevant features are identified; the way(s) in which they are similar/different is made clear and (where appropriate) the magnitude of the similarity/difference is noted.

4–6

AO1

4.6.2.3

4.6.2.4

Level 1: Relevant features are identified and differences noted.

1–3

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Similarities

Both processes can be used to modify/change/‘improve’ animals/plants/organisms.

Both processes involving choosing a genetic
characteristic and changing organisms so more have
the genetic characteristic.

Both processes have been used to improve food plants/domesticated animals.

Differences

In selective breeding characteristics are introduced by breeding parents with the desired characteristic(s); in genetic engineering characteristics are introduced by adding genes that have been ‘cut out’ from chromosomes.

In selective breeding characteristics/genes can only be introduced from other members of the same species; in genetic engineering characteristics/genes can be/are introduced from other species.

Selective breeding can take many generations; genetic engineering happens in one generation.

Selective breeding can lead to inbreeding; genetic engineering does not lead to inbreeding.

Selective breeding has been done for thousands of years; genetic engineering has only been done in recent years.

Genetic engineering sometimes involves bacteria; selective breeding does not (usually) involve bacteria.
sets.modelHtml: 28 Selective breeding is a way of using breeding to improve a plant or animal, for example making fruit bigger or tastier. It is done by choosing individuals with the features you want and breeding them together. For example, if you breed together a sheep with thick wool but poor meat and one with good meat but poor wool, you might get ones with good wool and good meat. Not all offspring will be like this, so you need to choose the best ones out of each generation and use these for breeding. Eventually after many generations you can get what you want. Genetic engineering is like this in that you can bring features together to improve an animal or plant, but the difference is that this is a modern technique that lets you combine features from different species that you couldn’t breed together. So you can cut out a gene say for disease resistance from one plant species and put it into another crop plant species so it won’t get the disease. This is a lot quicker than selective breeding because you don’t need to wait for lots of generations.
sets.partialHtml:
28 Both selective breeding and genetic engineering can be used to improve animals and plants. For example, to improve crop yields or make crops resistant to disease. Selective breeding is done by choosing two parents with the feature you want and breeding them together. Then choosing the offspring with the feature and breeding them together. After many generations all the animals or plants will have the feature you want. Genetic engineering is done by cutting out a gene from one organism and putting it in the cells of the organism you want to modify.

This answer describes one similarity and also describes the different ways each process is carried out. However, to gain full marks on an ‘evaluate’ question you need to clearly describe as many similarities and differences as you can. Although it is not necessary to include all the points in the mark scheme to gain full marks, for a 6-mark question more detail is needed. This answer therefore only gains Level 1.

2 out of 6 marks awarded.

29 The following notice appeared on social media.

Got a virus?

If you are feeling unwell you might have a virus.

Make sure you go to see your doctor and also make sure you ask for the antibiotics you need.

And don’t forget to finish the whole course.

Better safe than sorry!

Use your scientific knowledge to evaluate the advice given in the notice.

[6 marks]

parts.html:

Got a virus?

If you are feeling unwell you might have a virus.

Make sure you go to see your doctor and also make sure you ask for the antibiotics you need.

Better safe than sorry!

[6 marks]

Indicative content

Points in support of the notice

If you are unwell it might be because of a virus.

If you are unwell it might be best going to see your doctor (depending how ill you are).

You might need antibiotics if it’s a bacterial infection.

If you are prescribed antibiotics then you should finish the course

So all bacteria are killed and none survive to mutate and become resistant (to the antibiotic)

(Therefore) resistant bacteria may spread because there is no effective treatment.

Points against the notice:

If you are unwell then it might not be a virus / it could be a bacterial infection or some other illness.

If you are unwell it might be better to ring 111 (depending how ill you are).

You cannot use antibiotics against a viral infection.

Antibiotics are only used for bacterial infections.

Antibiotics are not prescribed for non-serious (bacterial) infections.

Inappropriate use of antibiotics can lead to the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria/strains

(Therefore) resistant bacteria may spread because there is no effective treatment.
sets.modelHtml: 29 There is some good advice and some bad advice in the notice. First, antibiotics do not work against viruses. They only work against bacteria. So they would be no good if you have a viral infection. The second thing is that even if you do have a bacterial infection you don’t always need antibiotics because often you will recover quickly anyway if it’s not serious. A doctor will only give out antibiotics if it’s a serious bacterial infection and you really need them, because if they are used too commonly then this can make it more likely that antibiotic-resistant bacteria will develop. The one good bit of advice in the notice is that if you are given antibiotics you should finish the course. This is to make sure all the bacteria are killed and none survive and become resistant.
sets.partialHtml:
29 Antibiotics only work against bacteria, so if you have a virus infection then they won’t do you any good at all. And you should only use antibiotics when they are really needed otherwise antibiotic-resistant bacteria can develop.

The student has made relevant comments about viral infections and the inappropriate use of antibiotics and has linked this to the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Although more detail could have been added, this is enough to gain Level 2. However, to gain Level 3 the student should also have commented on the rest of the notice. For example, there is some useful advice in the notice about finishing courses of antibiotics if you are prescribed them.

3 out of 6 marks awarded.

Woodlice prefer in order: dark and damp > dark and dry > light and damp > light and dry.

Overall woodlice prefer dark to light.

Overall woodlice prefer damp to dry.

Results fully support both aspects of the hypothesis that woodlice prefer dark and damp (to light and dry).

(Slightly) greater support for hypothesis that woodlice prefer dark to light, than for hypothesis that woodlice prefer damp to dry.

Shortcomings

Only limited amount of data.

Only small number/15 woodlice were tested.

Only counted on four occasions.

(At least some) woodlice were still clearly moving around

So the observed pattern(s) could have been anomalous.
sets.modelHtml: 30 Overall the results do support the hypothesis because the section with most woodlice in is consistently the dark damp one. However, although more woodlice prefer dark and damp than the other conditions, there are still those that prefer other conditions. In order, on average, 8.5 woodlice prefer dark and damp, 3.5 prefer dark and dry, 2.5 prefer light and damp, and 0.5 prefer light and dry, the least popular. If we add these together to compare dark and light, we get 12 in dark to 3 in the light, and 11 in damp to 4 in the dry. So it seems that although many prefer dark and damp, a fair number are happy with just one of these conditions. In favour of the results, there were 15 woodlice tested, and it was repeated 4 times, but against them perhaps it might be better to repeat it with more woodlice and also to leave it for longer in case they are still exploring the choice chamber before making a final decision where to stay. So overall the results do support the hypothesis, but further tests could be done to give it more weight.

The student has made a sensible judgement and has supported this with some appropriate calculations, so achieving Level 2. To move up to Level 3 the student should have included further points, such as describing some of the weaknesses in the data.

sets.title: Adaptations and evolution
sets.sourceHeading: Question (LD; Compare; Synoptic; Combined science)	Adaptations and evolution
sets.questionHtml:
31 The Galápagos islands are off the coast of South America.

Figure 15 shows two species of giant tortoise that live on different Galápagos islands.

One species has a saddleback shape shell with a high front.

The other species has a domed shape shell.

Both species evolved from smaller South American tortoises with a similar shape shell to the domed shell.

Figure 15

The saddleback tortoises live in dry habitats where there is very little vegetation close to the ground and they have to feed on tall vegetation.

The domed tortoises live in humid habitats where there is a lot of vegetation close to the ground to feed on.

31.1 Compare how the two types of shell have evolved.

[4 marks]

31.2 Describe how you could show that the two types of tortoise are different species.

[2 marks]

Indicative content

Similarities

Both types of shell are adaptations for survival.

Both are structural adaptations.

Both have evolved by natural selection.

Ancestors that had these shape shells were better suited to their environment (than other shapes)

And so were more likely to survive and pass on the feature to their offspring.

Both shell shapes allow tortoises to feed.

Both provide protection (against predators).

Differences

The saddleback shell is higher at the front than the
domed shell.

Tortoises with saddleback shells live in habitats with less/higher food than tortoises with domed shells.

The saddleback shell allows the tortoise to lift up its head/neck to feed on tall vegetation; the tortoise with the domed shell feeds on low vegetation so does not need to lift up its head/neck.

32.2

(Try to) breed them together.

If they do not produce fertile offspring they are different species.

sets.modelHtml: 31.1 Both types of shell have evolved by natural selection as adaptations to give the tortoises protection from predators. However, they also need to let the animals feed. There is no problem for the domed shell tortoises, who can feed on vegetation close to the ground. However, the saddleback tortoise needs to be able to stretch its neck up to reach food from the tall plants that grow where they live. To begin with they wouldn’t have been able to reach very high if they had a domed shaped shell, but any that were able to reach a bit higher than others because their shell was a bit higher at the front would get more food and so live longer to breed and pass on the genes for their shell shape. Over time therefore the shell would become more and more saddle shaped because each generation of those tortoises with shells that were higher at the front would have more offspring who would inherit that shape shell.
sets.partialHtml:

The student has made relevant points explaining how the two types of tortoise are different. This is enough for Level 1. However, no mention has been made of the similarities in how each adaptation evolved by natural selection.

2 out of 4 marks awarded.

sets.questionHtml:
32 Some students are investigating dandelion plants growing on a football pitch.

They want to estimate the total number of dandelion plants on the pitch.

Describe a method to do this.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
32 Some students are investigating dandelion plants growing on a football pitch.

They want to estimate the total number of dandelion plants on the pitch.

Describe a method to do this.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO /

Spec. ref.

32

Level 3: The method would lead to the production of a valid outcome. The key steps are identified and logically sequenced.

5–6

AO1

4.7.2.1

Level 2: The method would not necessarily lead to a valid outcome. Most steps are identified, but the method is not fully logically sequenced.

3–4

Level 1: The method plan would not lead to a valid outcome. Some relevant steps are identified, but links are not made clear.

1–2

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Measure the length of each side of the pitch

e.g. using a tape measure.

Calculate the area of the pitch.

Generate random coordinates (for both ‘axes’)

e.g. using numbers picked from a bag / random number table / random number generator.

Place the quadrat at point indicated by the coordinates.

Count the number of dandelion plants in the quadrat.

Count whole plants not separate leaves.

Only count plants that are rooted within the quadrat.

Repeat a suitable number of times / e.g.15 times.

Calculate the mean number of dandelion plants per quadrat or calculate the mean number of dandelion plants per m2.

Multiply the mean number of dandelion plants per quadrat by the number of times the area of the pitch is bigger than the area of the quadrat or multiply the mean number of dandelion plants per m2 by the area of the pitch.
sets.modelHtml: 32 First you need to measure the area of the football pitch. Use a tape measure in m to measure the length of one long side and one short side and multiply them together to give you the area in m2. Then measure the area of a quadrat in m2. Next you need to put the quadrat down in random places to avoid any bias. You can get random numbers from a computer programme and then use these to pick your spots. For example, if the random number is 2715 you go 27 m along one side, and 15 m along the other and see where the two lines meet, which is where you place the quadrat. You count how many dandelion plants are in the quadrat. Only count them if they are actually growing in the quadrat. Then repeat this for another 14 times. Work out the mean number of dandelion plants in one quadrat and then how many per m2. Multiply this number by the area of the pitch. This gives you an estimate for the number of dandelion plants on the pitch. The more quadrats you use to work out your mean, the more accurate your estimate will be.
sets.partialHtml:
32 You get your quadrat and put it down randomly on the football pitch. Count the number of dandelion plants in the quadrat and write it down. Put the quadrat down at another random coordinate and count the number of dandelions again. Repeat this say 10 times. Work out the average number of dandelions per quadrat and multiply up by the area of the football pitch. This will give you the total number of dandelions.

This answer gains Level 1. Many of the correct steps are referred to but not in enough detail for someone to follow this plan. For example, you would not multiply the mean number of dandelion plants per quadrat by the area of the football pitch. To gain a higher level they also need to explain exactly how they will generate the random coordinates for positioning the quadrats.

2 out of 6 marks awarded.

33 Many materials naturally cycle through ecosystems.

Describe how carbon is cycled through the natural world.

[6 marks]

parts.html:
33 Many materials naturally cycle through ecosystems.

Describe how carbon is cycled through the natural world.

[6 marks]

sets.schemeHtml:
Question

Answers

Mark

AO /

Spec. Ref.

33

Level 2: Scientifically relevant facts, events or processes are identified and given in detail to form an accurate account.

4–6

AO1

4.7.2.2

4.8

Level 1: Facts, events or processes are identified and simply stated but their relevance is not clear.

1–3

No relevant content

0

Indicative content

Carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is used/fixed by plants in photosynthesis

To make glucose/sugar/organic compounds.

Organic compounds are transferred to animals by eating.

Sugar/glucose/organic compounds are used (by plants and animals) in (cellular) respiration (to transfer/release energy)

Making carbon dioxide, which returns to the atmosphere.

Dead/waste remains are broken down/decayed/decomposed/respired

By microorganisms/bacteria

Returning carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.

Combustion of organic compounds

Makes carbon dioxide, which returns to the atmosphere.
sets.modelHtml: 33 Plants take in carbon dioxide from the atmosphere for photosynthesis. They use this to make glucose and then other foods such as starch or oil or protein. Some of the glucose they use in respiration and give out carbon dioxide again. Some of the plants are eaten by animals who take in the food and also use some for respiration so more carbon dioxide goes back into the air. Some dead plants and animals or waste do not get eaten but are decayed by microorganisms who also respire, putting carbon dioxide back into the air.
sets.partialHtml:
33 Carbon dioxide is taken in by plants when they photosynthesise. Then it’s passed on to animals when they eat them. The animals then breathe out the carbon dioxide again in respiration and it goes back into the air. More carbon dioxide goes back into the air when dead remains decay or when they are burned.

Although there are several correct, relevant points, there is one key error in that when animals eat plants they do not take in carbon dioxide (the animals take in the organic compounds that have been made by the plants in photosynthesis). This limits the answer to Level 1. To achieve Level 2, this needs to be corrected. Other details should also be included, for example the role of microorganisms.

3 out of 6 marks awarded.

sets.questionHtml:
35 Dinosaurs are a group of prehistoric reptiles that lived between about 230 million and 66 million years ago.

Scientists studying dinosaur fossils can tell whether they were herbivores or carnivores.

About 65% of fossil dinosaurs are herbivores and about 35% are carnivores.

Suggest explanations for this difference.

[6 marks]

Indicative content

Trophic levels

Herbivore dinosaurs are at the second trophic level/trophic level 2.

Carnivore dinosaurs are at the third or higher trophic level/trophic level 3 or higher.

There is less biomass at higher trophic levels.

Only about 10% of the biomass from one trophic level is transferred to the level above.

Losses of biomass are due to: not all ingested material is absorbed / some ingested material is egested as faeces; some absorbed material is lost as waste; large amounts of absorbed material/glucose are used in respiration.

(Therefore) there are (usually) fewer individuals at higher trophic levels.

(Therefore) you might expect about carnivore dinosaur fossils to be about 10% of the number of herbivore dinosaur fossils.

(However) this may not be the case if herbivore dinosaurs were much larger (on average) than carnivore dinosaurs, which would lead to a lower proportion of individual herbivore dinosaurs.

Carnivore dinosaurs might have eaten other things than herbivore dinosaurs.

Fossils

(Also) the fossil record is incomplete.

Many organisms never formed fossils / died in conditions/situations that did not lead to fossil formation.

Many fossils have not yet been discovered.

Many fossils have been destroyed by geological activity, e.g. by erosion.

Not all dinosaur fossils may be complete enough to identify as herbivore or carnivore.
sets.modelHtml: 35 You would expect there to be fewer carnivores than herbivores because that’s what we see today when there are almost always fewer predators than the prey they feed on. You can see this in pyramids of biomass where there is always less carnivore biomass than herbivore biomass in the trophic level below. The reason is that only about 10% of the biomass at each trophic level is transferred to the level above because the rest is either not eaten, is passed out as waste or is used up in respiration to get energy. So it makes sense that there are fewer carnivore dinosaurs than herbivores. However, in the case of the dinosaurs, 35 is not 10% of 65. This might be because we haven’t yet found all the dinosaur fossils, and we never will because not all dead animals form fossils (it’s very rare) and most fossils will never be found because they’ve either already been eroded or they are buried too deep.
sets.partialHtml:
35 There are lots of gaps in the fossil record because it is very hit and miss if a fossil forms in the first place and if it is ever found. So, the 65%/35% split might not be a true reflection of the numbers of actual dinosaurs. However, it makes sense that there are fewer carnivores than herbivores because in food webs usually there are fewer predators and more prey. This is because energy and biomass are lost from each level of a food chain and not passed on to the next. The way this shows itself is that there are fewer predators, e.g. there are fewer foxes than rabbits and fewer lions than zebras.

The student has given an ecological explanation as well as pointing out that the fossil record may not give a true picture of relative numbers. Enough relevant points have been made to gain Level 2. To gain Level 3 more detail is needed, for example, of the reasons why not all the biomass from one trophic level is passed to the next, or of why the fossil record is incomplete.

4 out of 6 marks awarded.
